title_original: Arnaldo Pappalardo: cópias fiéis dos cacos de nossos mundos
editorial_title_zh: Arnaldo Pappalardo：我们世界碎片的忠实副本
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在圣保罗苏马雷区一条繁忙的街道上，一家没有惯常的橱窗或门面屏障的店铺引人注目，因为它在外部的听觉与视觉混乱和内部安静的图像绿洲之间形成了鲜明对比。仿佛这个地方……

"在圣保罗苏马雷区一条繁忙的街道上，一家没有惯常的橱窗或门面屏障的店铺引人注目，因为它在外部的听觉与视觉混乱和内部安静的图像绿洲之间形成了鲜明对比。仿佛这个地方拥有自己的气场，随着那里展出的数十张照片每一次咔嚓声的节奏呼吸，并向每一位路人唱出无法抗拒的邀请，请他们踏上穿越其迷宫般领地的旅程——这片领地由各种领地的忠实副本、我们文明的碎片和漂浮世界的建筑构成。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个空间被命名为“Cópia Fiel”（忠实副本，致敬伊朗导演阿巴斯·基亚罗斯塔米（Abbas Kiarostami）的同名电影，该片将艺术作品原创性与复制的问题搬上银幕），它引导每位访客不仅对不同时间、空间与构图的细微与宏大获得诗意感知——这些都由其创始人 Arnaldo Pappalardo（圣保罗，1954）捕捉并再现。Cópia Fiel 于疫情后（2021）开幕，它不只是作者摄影的展览空间，更是由 Pappalardo 本人精心构思的真正装置，用来唤起、体验并揭示他近五十年作者创作中所拍摄图像之复制的本质。如今，这位圣保罗摄影师与视觉艺术家坚持在这个空间亲自接待每位访客，空间里布置着他从数千件收藏中挑选出的80幅摄影图像。正是在那里，他的一些旧日愿望得以实现：街道日常及其行人与其创作宇宙相连，任何人都能直接接触艺术家及其 dedicated 于艺术的空间，以及以民主且便利的方式购得照片。", Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arnaldo Pappalardo 毕业于圣保罗大学（USP）建筑系，但在进入大学之前，他从17岁起就已投身摄影。不过，正是在那里，当他开始频繁出入图书馆和摄影实验室，并接触摄影师兼教授 Cristiano Mascaro 和 João Luiz Musa 时，他才得以强化自己的眼光与摄影技术。与此同时，他还在造型艺术家 Carlos Fajardo 的工作室上素描和绘画课——这些技法此后一直被他用于摄影创作。由于他完全熟悉并置身于光所记录的世界以及更广泛意义上的造型艺术之中，毕业后他决定放弃建筑，以全部眼光与心灵投身摄影。从那时起，Pappalardo 在广告商业摄影领域建立了坚实且受认可的职业生涯。然而，他并未放弃自己的作者摄影创作——这引发了他对艺术家社会责任、艺术民主化及其市场壁垒、数字摄影和 AI 的思考。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“大约十年前，我的商业工作因多种原因逐渐停止：首先是因为数字摄影的整个问题以及图像开始被数字处理的方式，而更近些时候，我们又有了 AI 来生成图像。也就是说，我过去的工作方式，那种经典的摄影做法，几乎停摆了。因此，疫情期间我产生了一个疑问：从这里开始我要往哪里去？已经到了我必须第一次思考如何把我的作者作品作为摄影师进行商业化的时刻，因为在此之前，我完全靠商业摄影生活。趁着我有这个空间（Cópia Fiel），我开始把它设想为与街道完全相连、几乎是街道的延伸，没有门；人们可以自由进入，没有艺术画廊通常传递的那种令人畏惧的方面，我也可以在那里以非常可及的方式出售我的照片，不设限量版。毕竟，摄影允许无限复制”，艺术家回忆道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "利用自己的建筑学背景，Pappalardo 为 Cópia Fiel 设计并建造了每一件用于展示和保存其照片的家具。这些照片则不是获得艺术家的签名，而是获得其版权标识：保证这是原作的忠实副本，且经由艺术家本人之手。 “我不想强化艺术作品独占性的观念。我希望它体现可及性与亲近感的理念，正如瓦尔特·本雅明（Walter Benjamin）所指出的，摄影摧毁了传统艺术那种神秘而精英化的灵光。而正是为了再次打破那种令人畏惧的灵光概念，我亲自在这个空间接待每一个人。由于我漫长的职业生涯、我陆续举办的作者展览，以及我数十年作为广告摄影师的工作，很多人都听说过我的名字。当他们在这里看到我时，往往会吓一跳，因为他们曾把艺术家联想为难以接近的人。有了 Cópia Fiel，围绕艺术创作和艺术家的一切壁垒都被推倒了”，摄影师表示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在其创作实践中，帕帕拉尔多再次借助建筑（更确切地说，是通过其形式语汇，如平面、光与影、几何角度）让自己迷失并投身于城市迷宫般的小径，拾取那些在寻常目光下被忽略的图像片段：我们破碎世界的碎片。广告也为他发展影棚摄影技术提供了支撑。“比如在1980年代，我会在街上收集物件，把它们全都带到影棚，在那里搭景、布光并拍摄——完全是静物画的路子。广告在那部分技术上帮了我。”他回忆道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "观看帕帕拉尔多的每一幅图像，会发现尽管他从未以建筑师身份执业，建筑却已成为其摄影创作的重要方法，浸染并结构着他的目光。城市，连同它的迷宫与辽阔、生灵与幻影、具体与抽象，是他相当一部分作品中的反复出现的元素，例如他的项目《平静的张力》（由已停业的Cosac Naify出版社于2008年出版）。艺术家捕捉的每一处城市切片都跳动着其存在之力，构成关于当代大都市神话的视觉叙事，而这座都市的面貌并不容易被读取或破译。城市空间那些碎片化的面孔，与其说揭示并阐明其自身的历史与故事，不如说更多是在欺骗和使人迷失方向。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与经典的、本雅明式的漫游者形象相反——后者有意投身于城市中的闲逛，以便远距离凝视人群，并且仍能读解19和20世纪大都市的面貌（当时其立面、拱廊与地形仍透露着往昔的时代与故事）——帕帕拉尔多取的是相反的方向，在本质上成为一个“反漫游者”：他远离那个形象，因为他并非单纯的静观观察者，不是仅仅行走于当代城市、毫不费力地将其破译的人。相反，艺术家一头扎进这片疆域，去收集视觉符号、我们文明的碎片，正是通过它们，我们读取和破译其对我们破碎现实的忠实副本时的含混与困惑才得以显现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摩天楼的切片、无名的劳动者、孤独的人与动物、阴影与反光、沥青、橱窗、小径、招牌、窗户与门，构成一幅色彩、质地、高度与深度的马赛克，向我们眼中低语着帕帕拉尔多的多重感知，以图像反思城市环境中日常生活与社会关系的不可见性。“我的作品在关联图像的方式上由许多层次和复杂层级构成。照片本身彼此相当不同。对我而言，真正有意思的并不是按审美上的接近去关联它们，而是当两幅表面上极为不同的图像被并置时发生了什么。我的作品就发生在不同图像之间的这种关系与连接中。比如，当我意识到我四十年前拍的照片可以和我很久之后拍的其他照片关联起来时，这很有意思。", 2022年摄影书征集。它参照的是几十年前出版的那些知名手册，涉及裁剪的实践（在这里体现为图像之间的分隔）与缝纫的实践（在这里体现为图像被放在一起，仿佛被缝起来，以在它们之间创造一种叙事）。这部作品中图像之间的关联并非通过形式上明显相似来建立，而是通过它们之间的某种碰撞——仿佛只有从这种碰撞中，才能在观看者的思绪里创造出某种东西。因此，《手册》是一本对翻阅者要求很高的书。我喜歡这种无限关联序列的想法：在每一次新的翻阅中，都可能在一个永恒的游戏里发现新的叙事。同样的原则也出现在我另外两部摄影作品《碎片收藏》和《浮世》中”，艺术家指出。", "阿尔纳尔多·帕帕拉尔多《碎片收藏》系列全景", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《碎片收藏》（Coleção de Cacos）系列可被视为一件由400幅摄影图像碎片构成的万花筒，这些图像在最近10年间用同一台数码相机以小画幅拍摄，并被组织在一面由众多纵向和横向列构成的宽大墙面上。其中大多数图像是在圣保罗、巴黎、布拉格、伊斯坦布尔、博洛尼亚等多座城市的街道、公园、博物馆中拍摄的微距照片，他在这些地方寻找“通过对公共空间的细致观察而发现的敏感表面：正在被抹去、被时间作用所摧毁的图像，被遗忘的痕迹，它们甚至可能已经碎裂，如同瓷器的碎片”，帕帕拉尔多如是说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些被收集起来的碎片彼此并置，构成一部巨大的图像图集，其中的质感、色彩、来源与时间性以独特的方式交织在一起，将敏感表面与涂鸦的局部、绘画的细节、考古浮雕、天空或水中的细节混合，编织出一段独一无二的叙事。它的每一处截取都引导观者去检验的不只是自己既有的图像储备，还有自己的想象力——在靠近我们时代的废墟时，试着在它们之间建立联想。这一收藏中的每一块碎片都像一个独特的符号，构成整座大都市那多面而混杂的文本；由于构成它的视觉信息如洪水般涌来，这个文本混乱而难以被读取和辨认。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Colecao-de-Cacos-2.png?resize=1024%2C586&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《碎片收藏》系列局部，Arnaldo Pappalardo 作", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“《碎片收藏》的编辑手法以色彩作为各碎片之间的纽带，始终考虑每幅图像自身所唤起的敏感因素，以及它们之间某种程度的‘邻里亲和力’。就好像每张照片都是一块大织物上的一个细胞，构成一床在和谐与不和谐之间变化的拼布被，”帕帕拉尔多分析道。这种变化使观者产生一种需要：靠近又退远，以沉入这部图像图集再从中浮出——它把观者吸引进自身之中。“这是一次 zoom in 和一次 zoom out。当你靠近时，就像进入了每幅图像的复杂性之中。而当你退远时，形成的整体图像是一种拼布被，按我的估算，它大约有60米长，”他补充道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为构建这个项目，这位摄影师以德国艺术史学家阿比·瓦尔堡（Aby Warburg，1866-1929）的作品为参照：《摩涅莫绪涅图集》（Atlas Mnemosyne），这是欧洲文化研究中最激进、也未能完成的作品之一，因为其创作者在完成它之前便去世了。瓦尔堡制作了一系列黑色织物的大幅图板，在上面不加画框、不设主题层级、也不加固定说明文字地固定艺术品照片、星象图、印章、报纸剪报、广告、杂志图片——它们是他那个时代精神（Zeitgeist）的目击者。这些时代精神的碎片被摆放在大幅图板上，并不断被重新编排，正是为了不让它们陷入遗忘；也正因如此，他采用了《摩涅莫绪涅》这一标题，以纪念希腊的记忆女神、缪斯之母。对这位德国人而言，人类承载着一种近乎无意识的集体图像记忆（Bildgedächtnis），而他的图集将这种记忆物质化为一种制图学，它不遵循时间顺序或线性秩序，而是一种联想式、视觉性与关系性的关系，通过图像之间的关系性并置与碰撞来运作——正如帕帕拉尔多在《碎片收藏》中采用的方法。", "“在这里，图像的连接依靠色彩：三种原色、三种间色和复色。这个标题诞生于疫情期间，当时我开始给我在工作室里不断找到的一些木片涂色。我不知道自己是否有一天会展出这些绘画作品，但正是它催生了这面大型照片墙的标题。出于纯粹的好奇，有一天我在谷歌上搜索‘coleção de cacos’这个词，令我惊讶的是，我发现卡洛斯·德鲁蒙德·德·安德拉德有一首同名诗，它完全可以成为我作品的一段文本，因为这首诗讲的是不断碎裂的瓷器碎片，而某个人终有一天会把它们拼合起来。这种拼合碎片的行为与我作品中处理的东西相连：制造一种良性的、建设性的混乱，因为核心想法是你能够在这种混乱之中操作某些东西，构建新的宇宙。这里我想到法国精神分析学家费利克斯·瓜塔里的‘混沌互渗’（caosmose）概念：混沌作为一种从无序中创造的潜能。这与算法所引发的那种令人上瘾的、恶性的混乱毫无关系——算法操纵我们，最终什么也形不成。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "考虑到这种建设性混乱的观念，我非常喜欢比如一张大乌贼的照片旁边是一座巴洛克教堂。表面上看，一幅图像与另一幅毫无关系，但如果我们更仔细地观察每幅图像的轮廓，就会发现两者的细节确实彼此对话！当我发现这样奇怪的联想时，我感到极大的愉悦，因为在这种混乱的过程中产生了某种新东西，我无法用语言定义它，只能用图像，”帕帕拉尔多讲述道。", "translated": true}, {"type": · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "近年来不断激发这位艺术家的目光与心智的另一件作品，是装置《浮世》（Mundo Flutuante），其标题借自日本传统绘画与木版画浮世绘（Ukiyo-e）。它的雏形出现于1998年，最初是一次实验性创作：一张大画幅照片（一张20 x 25厘米的彩色透明片）被放入一个装有水的厨房耐热玻璃器皿中，并从下方打光。在器皿内部，这位艺术家还放入了水族箱小鱼，并拍摄了这个原型，用于他在一家画廊的展览。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“展览结束后，这件作品一直留在我脑海里，大约在2019年，我决定重新拾起它，但做了一些修改。我通过电影用的明胶片——一种彩色玻璃纸——在鱼缸结构的底部引入色彩。这些颜色变得有些模糊，仿佛我在不往水里倒颜料的情况下作画。此外，我还决定使用转印字母（受Mira Schendel启发）、小物件形状（比如印在塑料上并用激光切割的图标）、我用永久性马克笔绘制并覆膜的自绘图案（已经渗入水分并处于自然变化过程中），以及来自我商业作品死档案的剩余照片，以便自重启这个项目以来为这锅混合液增添更多实体感”，Pappalardo评论道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Mundo-Flutuante-1.png?resize=850%2C567&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Arnaldo Pappalardo的《Mundo Flutuante》系列", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就像一件玩具，《Mundo Flutuante》让观者任由自己漂流在一个模拟世界的顽皮把戏中，这个世界由实验和玩笑主宰，它们在这个小水库中安装的每一个水泡炸弹的作用时间里形成又变形。但是，撇开玩笑不谈，对创作者而言，这个世界涉及摄影宇宙起源的元语言。“水与摄影图像的互动，在某种程度上是一种元语言，因为所谓的模拟或光化学摄影诞生于水中，在暗房中冲洗胶片和放大照片的时刻”，他解释道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管这件作品和《Coleção de Cacos》一方面截然不同，另一方面却最终指向同一件事：图像在持续变化过程中彼此之间的关系。如果在《Coleção de Cacos》中，观者根据自己的世界观在图像之间形成各种各样的联想，那么在《Mundo Flutuante》中，置于水生环境中的图像则逃脱离观者的控制和注视，始终处于运动之中，按照自身的时间、冲动和机制形成并变形新的联想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Mundo-Flutuante-4.png?resize=850%2C567&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Arnaldo Pappalardo的《Mundo Flutuante》系列", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我一直在构建，而由于我已经71岁，有限性的念头开始触发。我不想离开这个迷宫，恰恰相反。我非常确信，正是在这些漂流中，一个人才能重新发明自己。对我来说，非常重要的是考虑到，艺术家最能具有革命性的时刻，是当他试图在语言问题上打破某些东西的时候。这是最让我感兴趣的那类艺术家：那种会让我感动的人，因为他在自身方式内部、在其艺术创作的裁缝铺里打破某些东西”，他补充道。在这个意义上，Arnaldo Pappalardo不仅是捕捉、切割和裁剪我们世界的角度与空间的参照，而且还能精准地拼合我们现实的碎片，让它们的裂缝不被察觉，以至于它们漂流、漂浮在一个混沌共生（caosmótico）的世界中，在一个创造性的混沌中，一个良性的混沌中。///", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Renata É como se esse lugar possuísse uma aura própria e respirasse no ritmo do click de cada uma das dezenas de fotografias ali exibidas e que cantam para todo transeunte um convite irresistível para empreender a travessia por seu território labiríntico construído com cópias fiéis de diversos territórios, cacos de nossa civilização e arquiteturas de mundos flutuantes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Esse espaço, batizado de Cópia Fiel (uma homenagem ao filme homólogo do diretor iraniano Abbas Kiarostami, que levou à tela a discussão sobre a originalidade e a cópia de obras de arte) conduz cada visitante não somente à percepção poética sobre miudezas e grandezas de diferentes tempos, espaços e composições captadas e reproduzidas por seu fundador, Arnaldo Pappalardo (São Paulo, 1954). Inaugurado pós-pandemia (2021), mais do que um espaço expositivo de fotografias autorais, Cópia Fiel é uma verdadeira instalação arquitetada minuciosamente pelo próprio Pappalardo para evocar, experimentar e revelar a essência da reprodução das imagens que fotografou ao longo de quase cinco décadas de produções autorais. Hoje, o fotógrafo e artista visual paulistano faz questão de receber cada visitante nesse espaço armado com 80 imagens fotográficas que selecionou entre milhares de sua coleção. É ali onde se concretizam alguns de seus antigos desejos como a conexão do cotidiano da rua e seus transeuntes com o seu universo criativo, o acesso direto de qualquer pessoa ao artista e ao seu espaço dedicado à arte, assim como à aquisição democrática e facilitada de fotografias."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Foto da série Cópia Fiel , de Arnaldo Pappalardo"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Copia-Fiel-4.png?resize=1024%2C683&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Foto da série Cópia Fiel , de Arnaldo Pappalardo", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Vista do espaço Cópia Fiel. Foto: Arnaldo Pappalardo"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Copia-Fiel-2.png?resize=1024%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Vista do espaço Cópia Fiel. Foto: Arnaldo Pappalardo", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Formado em Arquitetura na Universidade de São Paulo (USP), Arnaldo Pappalardo já vinha desde seus 17 anos se dedicando à fotografia antes de ingressar na faculdade. Mas foi ali, quando passou a frequentar a biblioteca e o laboratório fotográfico, assim como a ter contato com os fotógrafos e professores Cristiano Mascaro e João Luiz Musa, que pode intensificar seu olhar e técnicas fotográficas. Ao mesmo tempo, frequentou aulas de desenho e pintura no estúdio do artista plástico Carlos Fajardo – técnicas que, desde então, vem utilizando em suas criações fotográficas. Por estar plenamente familiarizado e inserido no mundo registrado pela luz e das artes plásticas de forma mais ampla, ao se formar decidiu abdicar da arquitetura para se dedicar de olho e alma à fotografia. A partir de então, Pappalardo construiu uma sólida e reconhecida trajetória como fotógrafo na área comercial da publicidade. No entanto, não renunciou à sua produção fotográfica autoral desde então – o que lhe gerou questionamentos sobre a consciência social da pessoa artista, a democratização da arte e os enclaves de seu mercado, da fotografia digital e IA."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Há aproximadamente uma década, meu trabalho comercial foi parando por vários motivos: primeiro porque começou toda a questão da fotografia digital e a maneira como as imagens passaram a ser manipuladas digitalmente e, mais recentemente, passamos a ter a IA para gerar imagens. Ou seja, a maneira como eu costumava trabalhar, a forma clássica de se fazer fotografia, praticamente parou. Por conta disso, me surgiu um questionamento durante a pandemia: Para onde eu vou a partir daqui? Tinha chegado o momento em que precisei pensar numa forma de comercializar pela primeira vez meu trabalho autoral como fotógrafo porque, até então, eu vivia exclusivamente da fotografia comercial. Aproveitando que eu tinha esse espaço (Cópia Fiel), comecei a pensá-lo totalmente conectado com a rua, quase que um prolongamento dela, sem porta; que as pessoas pudessem acessá-lo livremente sem o aspecto intimidatório que as galerias de arte costumam transmitir e onde pudesse vender minhas fotografias de uma maneira muito acessível, sem tiragem limitada. Afinal, a fotografia permite reproduções infinitas”, recorda o artista."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aproveitando sua formação em arquitetura, Pappalardo desenhou e construiu para Cópia Fiel cada móvel onde exibe e conserva suas fotografias. Elas, por sua vez, recebem, em vez da assinatura do artista, o seu copyright: a garantia de que se trata de uma cópia fiel da imagem original recebida pelas mãos do próprio artista. “Eu não quero reforçar a ideia da exclusividade de uma obra de arte. Quero que ela materialize a ideia de acessibilidade e proximidade, assim como Walter Benjamin apontou que a fotografia destruiu o aspecto de aura mística e elitista da arte tradicional. E, justamente para romper novamente com o conceito intimidatório da aura, recebo cada pessoa pessoalmente nesse espaço. Pela minha longa trajetória, a partir das exposições autorais que fui realizando e também pelo meu trabalho de décadas como fotógrafo publicitário, muitas pessoas já ouviram falar do meu nome. E quando me veem aqui, acabam levando um susto porque tinham feito a associação do artista como alguém de difícil acesso. Com Cópia Fiel, todas as barreiras em torno da criação artística e do artista são colocadas abaixo”, afirma o fotógrafo."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Em seu ofício criativo, Pappalardo faz novamente uso da arquitetura (mais precisamente através de seu repertório formal como planos, luz e sombras, ângulos geométricos) para se perder e se entregar às veredas labirínticas da urbe, colhendo recortes de imagens que passam despercebidamente ao olhar comum: cacos de nosso mundo fragmentado. A publicidade, por sua vez, também lhe serviu de apoio para desenvolver sua técnica de fotografia de estúdio. “Nos anos 1980, por exemplo, coletava objetos na rua e levava tudo para o estúdio, onde montava uma produção, iluminava e fotografava – bem no estilo da pintura de natureza morta. A publicidade me ajudou nessa parte técnica”, recorda."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo Pappalardo"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Tensao-Calma-2.png?resize=850%2C638&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo Pappalardo", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo PappalardoFoto da série Cópia Fiel , de Arnaldo Pappalardo"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Tensao-Calma-1.png?resize=609%2C850&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo PappalardoFoto da série Cópia Fiel , de Arnaldo Pappalardo", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo Pappalardo"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Tensao-Calma-3.png?resize=850%2C599&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo Pappalardo", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Observando cada imagem de Pappalardo, percebe-se que, embora nunca tenha atuado como arquiteto, a arquitetura tornou-se um importante método para sua criação fotográfica, impregnando e estruturando o seu olhar. A cidade, com seus labirintos e amplitudes, seres e fantasmagorias, concretudes e abstrações, é um elemento recorrente em boa parte do conjunto de sua obra, como no seu projeto Tensão Calma (com publicação pela extinta Editora Cosac Naify, 2008). Cada recorte da urbe captado pelo artista pulsa sua força existencial que compõe uma narrativa visual sobre a mitologia da cidade grande contemporânea e cuja fisiognomia não se deixa ser lida ou decifrada facilmente. As faces fragmentadas do espaço urbano mais enganam e desorientam do que revelam e esclarecem sua própria história e estórias que a compõem."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ao contrário da clássica figura do flâneur benjaminiano, que se entrega propositalmente a suas deambulações pela urbe para contemplar à distância a multidão e consegue ainda ler a fisiognomia da cidade grande dos séculos 19 e 20 (quando suas fachadas, passagens e topografias ainda revelavam épocas e estórias passadas), Pappalardo toma o sentido inverso, tornando-se um “anti-flâneur” em sua essência ao se distanciar da figura daquele por não ser um mero observador contemplativo, que simplesmente caminha pela cidade contemporânea, decifrando-a sem muito esforço. Pelo contrário, o artista se joga de cabeça nesse território para recolher signos visuais, fragmentos de nossa civilização, através dos quais são evidenciadas nossa imprecisão e confusão para ler e decifrar suas cópias fiéis de nossa realidade fragmentada."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Recortes de arranha-céus, trabalhadores anônimos, pessoas e animais solitários, sombras e reflexos, asfaltos, vitrines, trilhas, letreiros, janelas e portas compõem um mosaico de cores, texturas, alturas e profundidades que nos sussurra aos olhos as múltiplas percepções de Pappalardo para refletir com imagens a invisibilidade da vida cotidiana e das relações sociais no meio urbano. “O meu trabalho é composto por muitas camadas e níveis de complexidade na maneira de relacionar as imagens. As fotografias em si são bastante diferentes. Para mim, o que interessa não é exatamente associá-las por uma proximidade estética, mas o que acontece quando duas imagens, aparentemente muito diferentes entre si, são aproximadas. O meu trabalho acontece nessa relação e conexão entre imagens diferentes. Ele faz referência aos conhecidos manuais publicados décadas atrás, com as práticas de corte (aqui, presente na separação entre as imagens) e de costura (aqui, no fato das imagens terem sido colocadas juntas, como que costuradas, para a criação de uma narrativa entre elas). A associação entre as imagens desse trabalho não se dá pela semelhança formal e explícita, mas através de uma certa colisão entre elas – como que só a partir dessa colisão algo pudesse ser criado nos pensamentos de quem as vê. Uma loja sem as costumeiras barreiras de vitrines ou portas em uma rua movimentada do bairro paulista do Sumaré chama a atenção pelo contraste que forma entre o caos sonoro e visual de seu meio externo e o silencioso oásis imagético de seu ambiente interno. É como se esse lugar possuísse uma aura própria e respirasse no ritmo do click de cada uma das dezenas de fotografias ali exibidas e que cantam para todo transeunte um convite irresistível para empreender a travessia por seu território labiríntico construído com cópias fiéis de diversos territórios, cacos de nossa civilização e arquiteturas de mundos flutuantes.

Esse espaço, batizado de Cópia Fiel (uma homenagem ao filme homólogo do diretor iraniano Abbas Kiarostami, que levou à tela a discussão sobre a originalidade e a cópia de obras de arte) conduz cada visitante não somente à percepção poética sobre miudezas e grandezas de diferentes tempos, espaços e composições captadas e reproduzidas por seu fundador, Arnaldo Pappalardo (São Paulo, 1954). Inaugurado pós-pandemia (2021), mais do que um espaço expositivo de fotografias autorais, Cópia Fiel é uma verdadeira instalação arquitetada minuciosamente pelo próprio Pappalardo para evocar, experimentar e revelar a essência da reprodução das imagens que fotografou ao longo de quase cinco décadas de produções autorais. Hoje, o fotógrafo e artista visual paulistano faz questão de receber cada visitante nesse espaço armado com 80 imagens fotográficas que selecionou entre milhares de sua coleção. É ali onde se concretizam alguns de seus antigos desejos como a conexão do cotidiano da rua e seus transeuntes com o seu universo criativo, o acesso direto de qualquer pessoa ao artista e ao seu espaço dedicado à arte, assim como à aquisição democrática e facilitada de fotografias.

Foto da série Cópia Fiel , de Arnaldo Pappalardo

Vista do espaço Cópia Fiel. Foto: Arnaldo Pappalardo

Formado em Arquitetura na Universidade de São Paulo (USP), Arnaldo Pappalardo já vinha desde seus 17 anos se dedicando à fotografia antes de ingressar na faculdade. Mas foi ali, quando passou a frequentar a biblioteca e o laboratório fotográfico, assim como a ter contato com os fotógrafos e professores Cristiano Mascaro e João Luiz Musa, que pode intensificar seu olhar e técnicas fotográficas. Ao mesmo tempo, frequentou aulas de desenho e pintura no estúdio do artista plástico Carlos Fajardo – técnicas que, desde então, vem utilizando em suas criações fotográficas. Por estar plenamente familiarizado e inserido no mundo registrado pela luz e das artes plásticas de forma mais ampla, ao se formar decidiu abdicar da arquitetura para se dedicar de olho e alma à fotografia. A partir de então, Pappalardo construiu uma sólida e reconhecida trajetória como fotógrafo na área comercial da publicidade. No entanto, não renunciou à sua produção fotográfica autoral desde então – o que lhe gerou questionamentos sobre a consciência social da pessoa artista, a democratização da arte e os enclaves de seu mercado, da fotografia digital e IA.

“Há aproximadamente uma década, meu trabalho comercial foi parando por vários motivos: primeiro porque começou toda a questão da fotografia digital e a maneira como as imagens passaram a ser manipuladas digitalmente e, mais recentemente, passamos a ter a IA para gerar imagens. Ou seja, a maneira como eu costumava trabalhar, a forma clássica de se fazer fotografia, praticamente parou. Por conta disso, me surgiu um questionamento durante a pandemia: Para onde eu vou a partir daqui? Tinha chegado o momento em que precisei pensar numa forma de comercializar pela primeira vez meu trabalho autoral como fotógrafo porque, até então, eu vivia exclusivamente da fotografia comercial. Aproveitando que eu tinha esse espaço (Cópia Fiel), comecei a pensá-lo totalmente conectado com a rua, quase que um prolongamento dela, sem porta; que as pessoas pudessem acessá-lo livremente sem o aspecto intimidatório que as galerias de arte costumam transmitir e onde pudesse vender minhas fotografias de uma maneira muito acessível, sem tiragem limitada. Afinal, a fotografia permite reproduções infinitas”, recorda o artista.

Aproveitando sua formação em arquitetura, Pappalardo desenhou e construiu para Cópia Fiel cada móvel onde exibe e conserva suas fotografias. Elas, por sua vez, recebem, em vez da assinatura do artista, o seu copyright: a garantia de que se trata de uma cópia fiel da imagem original recebida pelas mãos do próprio artista. “Eu não quero reforçar a ideia da exclusividade de uma obra de arte. Quero que ela materialize a ideia de acessibilidade e proximidade, assim como Walter Benjamin apontou que a fotografia destruiu o aspecto de aura mística e elitista da arte tradicional. E, justamente para romper novamente com o conceito intimidatório da aura, recebo cada pessoa pessoalmente nesse espaço. Pela minha longa trajetória, a partir das exposições autorais que fui realizando e também pelo meu trabalho de décadas como fotógrafo publicitário, muitas pessoas já ouviram falar do meu nome. E quando me veem aqui, acabam levando um susto porque tinham feito a associação do artista como alguém de difícil acesso. Com Cópia Fiel, todas as barreiras em torno da criação artística e do artista são colocadas abaixo”, afirma o fotógrafo.

Em seu ofício criativo, Pappalardo faz novamente uso da arquitetura (mais precisamente através de seu repertório formal como planos, luz e sombras, ângulos geométricos) para se perder e se entregar às veredas labirínticas da urbe, colhendo recortes de imagens que passam despercebidamente ao olhar comum: cacos de nosso mundo fragmentado. A publicidade, por sua vez, também lhe serviu de apoio para desenvolver sua técnica de fotografia de estúdio. “Nos anos 1980, por exemplo, coletava objetos na rua e levava tudo para o estúdio, onde montava uma produção, iluminava e fotografava – bem no estilo da pintura de natureza morta. A publicidade me ajudou nessa parte técnica”, recorda.

Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo Pappalardo

Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo PappalardoFoto da série Cópia Fiel , de Arnaldo Pappalardo

Foto da série Tensão Calma , de Arnaldo Pappalardo

Observando cada imagem de Pappalardo, percebe-se que, embora nunca tenha atuado como arquiteto, a arquitetura tornou-se um importante método para sua criação fotográfica, impregnando e estruturando o seu olhar. A cidade, com seus labirintos e amplitudes, seres e fantasmagorias, concretudes e abstrações, é um elemento recorrente em boa parte do conjunto de sua obra, como no seu projeto Tensão Calma (com publicação pela extinta Editora Cosac Naify, 2008). Cada recorte da urbe captado pelo artista pulsa sua força existencial que compõe uma narrativa visual sobre a mitologia da cidade grande contemporânea e cuja fisiognomia não se deixa ser lida ou decifrada facilmente. As faces fragmentadas do espaço urbano mais enganam e desorientam do que revelam e esclarecem sua própria história e estórias que a compõem.

Ao contrário da clássica figura do flâneur benjaminiano, que se entrega propositalmente a suas deambulações pela urbe para contemplar à distância a multidão e consegue ainda ler a fisiognomia da cidade grande dos séculos 19 e 20 (quando suas fachadas, passagens e topografias ainda revelavam épocas e estórias passadas), Pappalardo toma o sentido inverso, tornando-se um “anti-flâneur” em sua essência ao se distanciar da figura daquele por não ser um mero observador contemplativo, que simplesmente caminha pela cidade contemporânea, decifrando-a sem muito esforço. Pelo contrário, o artista se joga de cabeça nesse território para recolher signos visuais, fragmentos de nossa civilização, através dos quais são evidenciadas nossa imprecisão e confusão para ler e decifrar suas cópias fiéis de nossa realidade fragmentada.

Recortes de arranha-céus, trabalhadores anônimos, pessoas e animais solitários, sombras e reflexos, asfaltos, vitrines, trilhas, letreiros, janelas e portas compõem um mosaico de cores, texturas, alturas e profundidades que nos sussurra aos olhos as múltiplas percepções de Pappalardo para refletir com imagens a invisibilidade da vida cotidiana e das relações sociais no meio urbano. “O meu trabalho é composto por muitas camadas e níveis de complexidade na maneira de relacionar as imagens. As fotografias em si são bastante diferentes. Para mim, o que interessa não é exatamente associá-las por uma proximidade estética, mas o que acontece quando duas imagens, aparentemente muito diferentes entre si, são aproximadas. O meu trabalho acontece nessa relação e conexão entre imagens diferentes. É interessante, por exemplo, quando percebo que imagens que fotografei há quarenta anos podem ser associadas a outras que fiz bem depois.

Warburg criou uma série de grandes painéis de tecido preto sobre os quais fixava, sem molduras, hierarquias temáticas ou legendas fixas, fotografias de obras de arte, mapas astrológicos, selos, recortes de jornais, anúncios, imagens de revistas – testemunhas oculares de seu Zeitgeist . Esses fragmentos do espírito de sua época dispostos sobre grandes painéis eram reorganizados constantemente, justamente para que não caíssem no esquecimento e, devido a isso, adotou o título ( Mnemosyne) em homenagem à deusa grega da Memória e mãe das Musas. Para o alemão, a humanidade carregava uma memória imagética coletiva ( Bildgedächtnis ) quase inconsciente e seu Atlas materializava uma cartografia dela, não seguindo uma ordem cronológica ou linear, mas sim uma relação associativa, visual e relacional, funcionando pela justaposição relacional e o choque entre imagens – tal como Pappalardo adota como método para sua Coleção de Cacos .

“Aqui, a articulação das imagens se dá pela cor: as três cores primárias, as três secundárias e as terciárias. Esse título surgiu durante a pandemia, quando comecei a pintar uns cacos de madeira que ia encontrando no meu estúdio. Não sei se algum dia vou expor esse trabalho de pintura, mas foi ele que gerou o título para esse grande painel de fotografias. Por pura curiosidade, pesquisei um dia no Google o termo ‘coleção de cacos’ e, para minha surpresa, descobri uma poesia de Carlos Drummond de Andrade com esse mesmo título e que poderia muito bem ser um texto para o meu trabalho porque o poema se refere a cacos de louça que vão quebrando e alguém, em algum dia, vai juntá-los. Esse ato de juntar cacos está conectado com o que estou tratando com a minha obra: produzindo um caos do bem e construtivo porque a ideia central é de que você possa operar alguma coisa dentro desse caos, construindo novos cosmos. Aqui penso no conceito de caosmose do psicanalista francês Félix Guattari: o caos como potência que cria a partir da desordem. Isso não tem nada a ver com o caos viciante e do mal provocado pelos algoritmos que nos manipulam e acabam não formando nada.

Considerando essa ideia de caos construtivo, gosto muito, por exemplo, da foto de uma lula grande ao lado de uma igreja barroca. Aparentemente, uma imagem não tem nada a ver com a outra, mas se observarmos com mais atenção os contornos de cada uma das imagens, percebemos que os detalhes de ambas dialogam sim entre si! Tenho um prazer muito grande quando descubro uma associação estranha como essa, porque algo novo se cria nesse processo caótico, que não consigo definir com palavras, somente com imagens”, relata Pappalardo.

Outro trabalho que vem instigando o olhar e a mente do artista nos últimos anos é a instalação Mundo Flutuante , cujo título foi emprestado da pintura e xilogravura tradicionais japonesas Ukiyo-e. Sua matriz surgiu em 1998 como uma produção-experimento: uma fotografia em grande formato (um cromo de 20 x 25 cm) colocada dentro de um pirex de cozinha com água e iluminada por baixo. Em seu interior, o artista colocou ainda peixinhos de aquário e fotografou esse protótipo para uma mostra sua em uma galeria.

“Passada a exposição, esse trabalho ficou na minha cabeça e, mais ou menos em 2019, decidi retomá-lo, mas com algumas modificações. Introduzi cores através de filtros de gelatina de cinema, uma espécie de folha colorida de celofane, na base da estrutura do aquário. Essas cores ficaram meio difusas, como se eu estivesse fazendo uma pintura sem jogar tinta na água. Além disso, decidi também usar letras decalcadas (inspiração de Mira Schendel), pequenas formas de coisas (tipo ícones impressos sobre plástico e cortados a laser), desenhos meus feitos com caneta permanente e plastificados (já com infiltração da água e em processo natural de modificação) e fotografias de sobras de um arquivo-morto com meus trabalhos comerciais para dar mais corpo a esse caldo desde a retomada desse projeto”, comenta Pappalardo.

Assim como um brinquedo, Mundo Flutuante leva o observador a se entregar à deriva nas traquinagens de um mundo analógico regido por experimentos e bromas que se formam e se desformam no tempo de ação de cada uma das bombinhas de água instalada nesse pequeno reservatório de água. Mas, deixando as brincadeiras à parte, para o criador, esse mundo trata de uma metalinguagem da cosmogonia da fotografia. “A interação da água com as imagens fotográficas, em parte, trata-se de uma metalinguagem, já que a fotografia dita analógica ou fotoquímica nasce na água, no momento da revelação dos filmes e das ampliações fotográficas em laboratório”, explica.

Embora esse trabalho e Coleção de Cacos sejam, por um lado, absolutamente diferentes, por outro, acabam se referindo à mesma coisa: à relação das imagens entre si em um processo constante de mudança. Se em Coleção de Cacos o observador forma associações das mais variadas entre as imagens em conformidade com sua própria cosmovisão, em Mundo Flutuante as imagens dispostas em um meio aquático fogem ao controle e da mirada do observador, estando a todo momento em movimento, formando e deformando novas associações regidas por seus próprios tempos, pulsões e mecanismos.

“Estou construindo o tempo todo e, como estou com 71 anos, a ideia da finitude começa a disparar. Não quero sair desse labirinto, pelo contrário. Tenho muito uma certeza de que é nessas derivas onde uma pessoa pode se reinventar. Para mim é muito importante considerar que onde o artista pode ser mais revolucionário é quando tenta quebrar alguma coisa na questão da linguagem. Esse é o tipo de artista que mais me interessa: aquele que vai me emocionar porque está quebrando algo dentro da própria maneira, de sua alfaiataria do fazer artístico”, complementa. Nesse sentido, Arnaldo Pappalardo não somente é uma referência em capturar, cortar e recortar ângulos e espaços de nosso mundo, mas de juntar com precisão os cacos de nossa realidade sem que suas fissuras possam ser notadas, a ponto de ficarem à deriva, flutuando em um mundo caosmótico , em um caos criativo, um caos do bem. ///

Renata Martins (1980) é educadora, crítica de arte e curadora independente natural de São Paulo. É mestre em Literatura Alemã pela USP e especialista em Curadoria de Arte pela Universidade das Artes de Berlin. Foi residente do programa Vila Sul do Instituto Goethe de Salvador (2020-2022), onde concebeu e organizou o Catálogo Arte Mais – Panorama de Artistas Transvestigeneres no Brasil @catalogoartemais .

"这种合作方法也体现在机构之间实际相互支持的方式中。各个组织公开分享了关于观众行为、项目成功与挑战以及其他运营经验的见解。邓迪当代艺术中心（Dundee Contemporary Arts）与爱丁堡雕塑工坊（Edinburgh Sculpture Workshop）等机构之间的合作协议也给我留下了深刻印象，这些协议允许任一机构的关联艺术家使用共享的制作设施与资源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这段经历巩固了我的信念：当机构和从业者将自己视为更广阔生态系统的一部分，而非孤立的实体时，艺术领域就会繁荣发展。当艺术家、机构、资助方、大学和政府机构协同合作时，他们不仅能强化自身的组织，还能增强整个文化部门。这也让我不禁思考，我们如何在沙特阿拉伯培育类似的对话空间，无论是通过正式论坛还是非正式聚会，让文化从业者能够讨论共同的挑战、交流想法，并从彼此的成功与挫折中学习。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目的结构是如何促进真正的交流或合作，而不是单向的观点呈现的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在参访之前，我对苏格兰艺术界的了解相对有限。在为期6天的时间里，该项目通过参访格拉斯哥、邓迪、爱丁堡、布特岛、罗斯内斯半岛及周边地区的机构和画廊，提供了对该行业的全面概述。我们参观了11家文化机构，并参加了3场行业会议，这不仅让我们深入了解了每个组织的使命与节目策划，还了解了它们的治理结构、运营模式以及领导文化机构的日常现实。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让这段经历特别有意义的是，它促进了真正的双向交流。与苏格兰创意局（Creative Scotland）视觉艺术主管艾玛·尼科尔森（Emma Nicolson）、邓迪当代艺术中心总监贝丝·贝特（Beth Bate）、霍斯菲尔德（Hospitalfield）总监露西·拜亚特（Lucy Byatt）、塔尔博特赖斯画廊（Talbot Rice Gallery）总监苔丝·吉布林（Tessa Giblin）等众多从业者的对话迅速超越了展示汇报，转变为关于各自文化部门的公开讨论。虽然我们渴望了解他们在资助、治理和文化领导力方面的方法，但他们同样有兴趣了解沙特阿拉伯视觉艺术生态系统的迅猛发展。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "许多人解释说，他们一直在远程关注沙特阿拉伯的发展，但希望更好地理解是什么在推动这一转型，公私机构之间的关系如何演变，以及从业者如何展望该行业的未来。这些对话也显露出了实地访问沙特阿拉伯并亲身体验艺术现场的真诚好奇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目没有采用单向的观点呈现，而是为对话、反思和相互学习创造了空间，彰显了文化交流作为持久合作基石的价值。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于沙特阿拉伯和苏格兰当代艺术生态系统之间的相似性或差异，最让你惊讶的是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我观察到苏格兰和沙特艺术生态系统中都存在强烈的场所连结感。尽管我们的文化和历史背景不同，但两国艺术家都深深地投入到他们的本土环境、历史、身份以及塑造其社区的社会变革之中。在这两种情况下，艺术都充当了记录、反思和质疑这些转型的一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "许多机构扮演社区枢纽而非单纯的展览空间这一角色也令我震撼。在整个苏格兰，我们遇到了积极在当地社区内促进对话、学习和参与的组织。这与沙特阿拉伯正在涌现的许多倡议产生了共鸣，在那里的艺术家和文化从业者同样致力于支持和强化其本土生态系统。
该项目强化了我的信念：最有意义的文化机构是那些既扎根于社区、又为更广泛的对话与交流创造空间的机构。
苏格兰艺术界的哪个方面促使你重新思考如何在不断发展的沙特视觉艺术背景下演变或调整类似结构？
一个关键收获是多元化支持系统的重要性。虽然公共资助发挥着至关重要的作用，但赞助人、个人捐赠者和社区支持者的作用同样意义重大。
我们参访的机构表明，一个蓬勃发展的文化部门不能单靠公共资助。它还需要来自更广泛社区的投资——那些相信艺术价值并通过慈善事业、倡导和积极参与来支持它的人们。
随着沙特阿拉伯视觉艺术持续发展，我相信有机会在现有公共支持的同时，培育更强大的赞助和个人捐赠文化。建立这种共享所有权感，不仅对各个机构的可持续性至关重要，对于更广阔文化生态系统的长期韧性与发展也必不可少。
你认为该项目潜在的长期影响是什么？
我相信最有价值的成果之一是在沙特阿拉伯和苏格兰的文化从业者之间建立的关系网络。通过对包括苏格兰创意局、邓迪当代艺术中心、爱丁堡雕塑工坊、塔尔博特赖斯画廊、朱庇特艺术乐园（Jupiter Artland）等机构的参访和讨论，我们建立起了建立在坦诚、信任以及对强化各自文化部门共同承诺之上的关系。
我们的许多对话自然而然地转向了未来的机构合作。通过知识交流、联合策划、专业交流以及建立长期机构伙伴关系的机遇，加强沙特阿拉伯与苏格兰文化组织之间的关系产生了真诚的兴趣。我们还讨论了围绕文化领导力、资助模式、公私机构之间关系以及可持续当代艺术生态系统发展的持续知识交流。几位从业者还表达了访问沙特阿拉伯的强烈兴趣，以亲身体验他们此前大体上只能远程关注的转型。
除了具体项目之外，我认为该项目创造了同样重要的成果：对不同的文化生态系统如何运作以及它们能向彼此学习什么有了更深理解。这类交流拓宽了视野、挑战了既定假设，并为有意义的长期合作奠定了必不可少的信任基础。
回顾你的经历，关于像“艺术之桥”这样的项目所开启的未来可能性，你想向组织者、东道主甚至你自己提出什么问题？
我向自己提出的问题是：我该如何帮助维持和扩大通过该项目建立的联系，从而为两国艺术家和文化从业者带来有意义的机遇？
项目的真正影响将由接下来发生的事情来衡量。涌现出的关系、对话和想法有可能演变为未来的合作、展览、交流和专业伙伴关系。
对我而言，挑战在于思考如何随着时间推移培育这些联系，并将其转化为沙特阿拉伯和苏格兰艺术家、机构和文化从业者的切实机遇。“艺术之桥”这样的项目之所以重要，是因为它们为对话奠定了基础；我们（参与者）所有人都有责任在此基础上继续建设，并确保交流保持活跃、具相关性且互利共赢。

I was impressed by how deeply community engagement was embedded within the curatorial process, with exhibitions and public programs developed alongside communities. “Thread Memory: Embroidery from Palestine” was a powerful example, demonstrating how collaborative curation can center community voices, preserve cultural heritage, and create meaningful opportunities for dialogue and reflection. article_text:
People

Community and Sustainability: Notes from Scotland

AHAAD ALAMOUDI ,

GAIDA ALMOGREN ,

MAHMOUD SAMI ,

ABDULLAH ALAMOUDI ,

ABDULMOHSEN ALBINALI ,

IBRAHIM ROMMAN ,

BAYAN ASHOUR ,

DANYA FAISAL ,

AFIA BIN TALEB , and

HAFSA ALKHUDAIRI , participants of the Art Bridges Scotland program, held from Sep 22–27, 2025.

In September 2025, Saudi Arabia’s Visual Arts Commission sent a delegation of artists and cultural practitioners to Scotland through Art Bridges, a professional development program connecting participants with international peers. Visits to cultural institutions and conversations with Scottish practitioners led to in-depth reflections on approaches to community engagement, institutional collaboration, and sustainability in visual arts.

Below, Danya Faisal, Bayan Ashour, and Afia Bin Taleb reflect on the exchange and the possibilities it opened for Saudi Arabia’s growing visual arts sector.

DANYA FAISAL

Danya Faisal is community relations coordinator at Hayy Jameel in Jeddah overseeing community outreach programs, managing communication platforms, and fostering collaborations.

DANYA FAISAL at Dundee, Scotland, during the Art Bridges Scotland program, Sep 22–27, 2025.

Can you describe a specific moment during the program when a conversation or interaction changed the way you think about the role of visual arts in society?

A conversation with Leonie Bell, director of V&A Dundee, about museums as spaces for public dialogue rather than simply venues for exhibiting collections stands out for me. I was impressed by how deeply community engagement was embedded within the curatorial process, with exhibitions and public programs developed alongside communities. “Thread Memory: Embroidery from Palestine” was a powerful example, demonstrating how collaborative curation can center community voices, preserve cultural heritage, and create meaningful opportunities for dialogue and reflection. The conversation shifted my understanding of the social role of visual arts and reinforced the idea that cultural institutions can actively shape public memory and discourse.

How did the program’s structure foster genuine exchange or collaboration, rather than a one-way presentation of ideas?

The program encouraged dialogue, creating opportunities to exchange ideas with museums, galleries, universities, and artists across Scotland. Discussions centered on the evolving role of museums as spaces for public engagement, community-led curation, cultural representation, and preserving heritage. We explored how institutions address inclusivity, accessibility, and contemporary social issues through exhibitions and programming. Conversations also examined artistic research, interdisciplinary practice, and audience participation. A conversation I had with Tessa Giblin from the Talbot Rice Gallery proved that Scottish practitioners were equally interested in learning about Saudi Arabia’s rapidly developing cultural sector, making the exchange collaborative and reciprocal.

What most surprised you about the similarities or differences between the contemporary art ecosystems in Saudi Arabia and Scotland?

What surprised me most was how many similarities existed between the contemporary art communities despite differences in scale and institutional history. Artists in both Saudi Arabia and Scotland are engaging with themes of identity, heritage, and social change, but the methods and approaches being used differ. In Scotland, I found that arts institutions were closely integrated with their local communities through public programs and accessible engagement. Seeing this encouraged me to think about how Saudi cultural spaces might continue growing through more participatory and community-centered approaches.

Did any aspect of the Scottish art scene prompt you to reconsider how similar structures might evolve or be adapted within the growing Saudi visual arts context?

Yes, the Scottish art scene made me consider the role that museums and galleries in Saudi Arabia might play, especially when it comes to accessibility and public engagement. I was particularly interested in how institutions like the Dundee Contemporary Arts balanced academic rigor with experimentation and community interaction. The relationship between artists, curators, and audiences often felt open and conversational. It made me think about how Saudi institutions can continue growing while remaining responsive to local communities and cultural contexts. Rather than simply adopting external institutional models, I believe Saudi Arabia is actively working to develop its own approaches that combine local values with collaborative and experimental practices.

What do you see as the potential long-term impacts of the program?

The program created valuable opportunities for artists and cultural practitioners from different backgrounds to openly discuss their practices, challenges, and aspirations. One of the most insightful conversations was with the leadership team at Cove Park, where we explored the role and impact of artist residencies in supporting creative development, collaboration, and experimentation. As artist residency programs continue to grow within Saudi Arabia’s cultural sector, these discussions were particularly relevant to my role at Art Jameel and reinforced my interest in expanding residency opportunities within our own organization. While these conversations may lead to future collaborations, the program’s greatest impact was in reshaping my understanding of cultural exchange. Rather than focusing solely on institutional partnerships, it emphasized dialogue, mutual curiosity, and shared learning.

Reflecting on your experience, what is one question you wish to pose to the organizers, the hosts, or even to yourself about the future possibilities opened by programs like Art Bridges?

Reflecting on the experience, the main question I would ask is: how can programs like Art Bridges create longer-term collaborative ecosystems rather than short-term exchanges? The program demonstrated the value of dialogue and exposure to new cultural contexts, but it also highlighted the importance of continuity. I would be interested in exploring how relationships developed through programs like this could evolve into sustained partnerships, co-curated projects, or reciprocal residency opportunities.

BAYAN ASHOUR

Bayan Ashour is visitor experience manager at Hayy Jameel in Jeddah. Her work focuses on audience engagement and making art accessible and welcoming to diverse communities.

BAYAN ASHOUR (right) at V&A, Scotland, during the Art Bridges Scotland program, Sep 22–27, 2025.

Can you describe a specific moment during the program when a conversation or interaction changed the way you think about the role of visual arts in society?

Encounters at Tramway and Trongate 103 served as profound catalysts for rethinking the civic potential of creative institutions. Witnessing them operate, not merely as venues but as vital spaces, was a revelation. It mirrored our ambitions at Hayy Jameel, to cultivate a site that belongs, fundamentally, to its community. I realized that a visitor’s journey should transcend the formal, pristine gallery into an immersion within a vibrant creative ecosystem. This experience crystallized my objective: to move beyond the logistics of audience management toward the cultivation of a warm, inclusive environment where practitioners from all disciplines feel empowered to gather, discourse, and co-create.

How did the program’s structure foster genuine exchange or collaboration, rather than a one-way presentation of ideas?

During the program, moving from the storied halls of The Burrell Collection to the immersive landscape of Cove Park, and finally to V&A Dundee, facilitated an organic kinship rather than a traditional institutional exchange. We found ourselves in a sophisticated, two-way dialogue regarding the architecture of welcome, support, and empowerment. It was never a unidirectional lecture; our Scottish peers were equally intrigued by the energetic, community-led ethos defining Hayy Jameel. At Dundee Contemporary Arts, our discussions on public engagement became a rich tapestry of shared narratives, exploring how to invite families and independent thinkers into our spaces as partners in authorship, ensuring that contemporary art remains a radical, accessible commons for all.

What most surprised you about the similarities or differences between the contemporary art ecosystems in Saudi Arabia and Scotland?

I was struck by the realization that creative impulses remain universal, transcending geographic and cultural specificities. Whether at a grassroots incubator like the Edinburgh Sculpture Workshop or within a multidisciplinary framework like Hayy Jameel, there is a shared, restless curiosity to convene and create.

Did any aspect of the Scottish art scene prompt you to reconsider how similar structures might evolve or be adapted within the growing Saudi visual arts context?

In Scotland, museums often function as public squares where casual connection and quiet contemplation are valued as deeply as the art itself. This inclusive social architecture offers a compelling blueprint for our rapidly growing Saudi visual arts landscape where institutions can operate as civic “green lungs”—social sanctuaries that are vital to the urban fabric.

Observing how they function completely reshaped how I approach visitor experience and audience engagement. Seeing how these institutions have built hospitality directly into their physical layouts and public programming showed me how to break down the intimidation surrounding contemporary art.

Bringing these open, welcoming strategies to Hayy Jameel means looking at the whole visitor journey, from opening our gallery thresholds into the central courtyard (Saha) to rethinking how we guide people through exhibitions. A direct result of this was our new “From Another Angle” tour format. Rather than delivering a traditional lecture, these tours invite visitors to actively analyze, question, and connect with contemporary art through open dialogue, understanding artists’ perspectives contextually and conceptually.

Combining these interactive touchpoints with an accessible environment shifts the experience from passive viewing to genuine belonging, turning Hayy Jameel into a lively, everyday hub for community and culture.

What do you see as the potential long-term impacts of the program?

This exchange transcended from professional development, establishing a resilient framework for bilateral, co-curatorial dialogue. Beyond institutional frameworks, we cultivated an organic “community of care.” Witnessing how Scottish institutions view the public as collaborative partners rather than a mere demographic profoundly rewired our approach to creative engagement. The enduring legacy of this program lies in building inclusive creative districts where creative initiatives thrive, ensuring that as our respective ecosystems mature, community agency remains at the absolute core of our practice.

Reflecting on your experience, what is one question you wish to pose to the organizers, the hosts, or even to yourself about the future possibilities opened by programs like Art Bridges?

We benefited from incredible hospitality and connection. The one question I want to ask is how we can translate the momentum of this exchange into a daily practice that ensures Hayy Jameel remains a truly accessible and empowering home for our community. The program ignited a wonderful spark; the true work ahead lies in ensuring that the strategies we experienced can continue to inspire and soften the spaces we manage back home every single day.

AFIA BIN TALEB

Afia Bin Taleb is a Jeddah-based independent cultural advisor and former director of ATHR Gallery. Her work focuses on institutional strategy, programming, and partnerships in contemporary art.

AFIA BIN TALEB (left) sharing ideas with fellow participants

AHAAD ALAMOUDI and

ABDULLAH ALAMOUDI , co-founders of the SINDBAD Collective, during a visit to Mount Stuart on the Isle of Bute, during the Art Bridges Scotland program, Sep 22–27, 2025.

Can you describe a specific moment during the program when a conversation or interaction changed the way you think about the role of visual arts in society?

The roundtable discussions held at the end of each city visit, which brought together cultural practitioners, institutional leaders, and decision-makers, were among the most impactful aspects of the program. What struck me was that many of the challenges they are facing are remarkably similar to those we encounter in Saudi Arabia, ranging from operational constraints to audience engagement.

The openness with which these challenges were discussed was striking. There was a strong sense of transparency and collective responsibility. Cultural leaders were committed to sharing knowledge and learning from one another. This culture of exchange and mutual support was inspiring and instructive.

The collaborative approach was also reflected in the way institutions practically supported one another. Organizations openly shared insights into audience behaviour, programming successes and challenges, and other operational learnings. I was also impressed by collaborative agreements between institutions such as Dundee Contemporary Arts and Edinburgh Sculpture Workshop, which allow artists affiliated with either organization to access shared production facilities and resources.

The experience reinforced my belief that the arts sector thrives when institutions and practitioners view themselves as part of a broader ecosystem rather than as individual entities. When artists, institutions, funders, universities, and government agencies work collaboratively, they strengthen not only their own organizations but the cultural sector as a whole. It also left me wondering how we might foster similar spaces for dialogue in Saudi Arabia, whether through formal forums or informal gatherings, where cultural practitioners can discuss shared challenges, exchange ideas, and learn from one another’s successes and setbacks.

How did the program’s structure foster genuine exchange or collaboration, rather than a one-way presentation of ideas?

Before the visit, my knowledge of the Scottish art scene was relatively limited. Over the course of six days, the program provided a comprehensive overview of the sector through visits to institutions and galleries across Glasgow, Dundee, Edinburgh, the Isle of Bute, the Rosneath Peninsula, and surrounding areas. We visited 11 cultural institutions and participated in three sector meetings, which offered insights not only into each organization’s mission and programming, but also into their governance structures, operational models, and the day-to-day realities of leading cultural institutions.

What made the experience particularly meaningful was that it fostered a genuine two-way exchange. Conversations with practitioners such as Emma Nicolson, head of visual arts at Creative Scotland, Beth Bate, director of Dundee Contemporary Arts, Lucy Byatt, director of Hospitalfield, and Tessa Giblin, director of Talbot Rice Gallery, and many more, quickly moved beyond presentations and became open discussions about our respective cultural sectors. While we were eager to learn about their approaches to funding, governance, and cultural leadership, they were equally interested in understanding the rapid development of Saudi Arabia’s visual arts ecosystem.

Many explained that they had been following developments in Saudi Arabia from afar but wanted to better understand what was driving this transformation, how relationships between public and private institutions were evolving, and how practitioners envisioned the future of the sector. These conversations also revealed a genuine curiosity to visit Saudi Arabia and experience the art scene firsthand.

Rather than a one-way presentation of ideas, the program created a space for dialogue, reflection, and mutual learning, highlighting the value of cultural exchange as the foundation for lasting collaboration.

What most surprised you about the similarities or differences between the contemporary art ecosystems in Saudi Arabia and Scotland?

I observed a strong sense of connection to place in both the Scottish and Saudi art ecosystems. Despite our different cultural and historical contexts, artists in both countries are deeply engaged with their local environments, histories, identities, and the social changes shaping their communities. In both cases, art serves as a means of documenting, reflecting on, and questioning these transformations.

I was also struck by the role that many institutions play as community hubs rather than simply exhibition spaces. Across Scotland, we encountered organizations that were actively fostering dialogue, learning, and participation within their local communities. This resonated with many initiatives emerging in Saudi Arabia, where artists and cultural practitioners are equally committed to supporting and strengthening their local ecosystems.

The program reinforced my belief that the most meaningful cultural institutions are those that remain rooted in their communities while creating space for broader conversations and exchange.

Did any aspect of the Scottish art scene prompt you to reconsider how similar structures might evolve or be adapted within the growing Saudi visual arts context?

A key takeaway was the importance of a diversified support system. While public funding plays a crucial role, the role of patrons, individual donors, and community supporters is just as significant.

The institutions we visited demonstrated that a thriving cultural sector cannot rely on public funding alone. It also requires investment from the wider community—people who believe in the value of the arts and are willing to support it through philanthropy, advocacy, and active participation.

As Saudi Arabia’s visual arts sector continues to grow, I believe there is an opportunity to cultivate a stronger culture of patronage and individual giving alongside existing public support. Building this sense of shared ownership will be essential not only for the sustainability of individual institutions but also for the long-term resilience and development of the broader cultural ecosystem.

What do you see as the potential long-term impacts of the program?

I believe one of the most valuable outcomes is the network of relationships that was established between cultural practitioners in Saudi Arabia and Scotland. Through our visits and discussions with organizations including Creative Scotland, Dundee Contemporary Arts, Edinburgh Sculpture Workshop, Talbot Rice Gallery, Jupiter Artland, and others, we developed relationships built on openness, trust, and a shared commitment to strengthening our respective cultural sectors.

Many of our conversations naturally turned towards future institutional collaboration. There was genuine interest in strengthening relationships between cultural organizations in Saudi Arabia and Scotland through knowledge exchange, joint programming, professional exchanges, and opportunities for long-term institutional partnerships. We also discussed continued knowledge exchange around cultural leadership, funding models, the relationship between public and private institutions, and the development of sustainable contemporary art ecosystems. Several practitioners also expressed a strong interest in visiting Saudi Arabia to experience firsthand the transformation they had largely followed from afar.

Beyond specific projects, I think the program created something equally important: a deeper understanding of how different cultural ecosystems operate and what they can learn from one another. These kinds of exchanges broaden perspectives, challenge assumptions, and create the trust that is essential for meaningful long-term collaboration.

Reflecting on your experience, what is one question you wish to pose to the organizers, the hosts, or even to yourself about the future possibilities opened by programs like Art Bridges?

The question I pose to myself is: How can I help sustain and expand the connections created through this program so that they lead to meaningful opportunities for artists and cultural practitioners in both countries?

The true impact of the program will be measured by what happens next. The relationships, conversations, and ideas that emerged have the potential to evolve into future collaborations, exhibitions, exchanges, and professional partnerships.

For me, the challenge is to think about how these connections can be nurtured over time and translated into tangible opportunities for artists, institutions, and cultural practitioners in both Saudi Arabia and Scotland. Programs like Art Bridges are important because they create the foundation for dialogue; it is up to all of us (participants) to continue building on that foundation and ensure that the exchange remains active, relevant, and mutually beneficial.

This article is part of a special series exploring Art Bridges, the Visual Arts Commission’s international exchange program connecting Saudi and Saudi-based artists and cultural practitioners with peers in Scotland, South Korea, Japan, and Spain.

World”项目以及打造该项目的人们交织在一起，迫使他不得不去直面自己一直背负的失落。正是在这些抗拒日常表达的体验中，艺术变得最具意义：例如一幅画，“它是一个不需要解释的真理。没有贵族，没有象征主义，没有谎言。一幅清晰如爱的画作”；还有一次，当叙述者的朋友将怀孕的经历比作他们曾在博物馆见过的一幅画时，“那里的色彩更强烈、更明亮，有一种质感。就像打破了一道屏幕，世界感觉变大了，仿佛无法被容纳”。", article_text:
For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, the art critic’s debut novel remains surprisingly sincere about art itself

The unnamed narrator of Ben Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World , is, like Eastham himself , an art critic. Grieving his recently deceased wife, he feels lost while teaching at a school where the students refer to him as ‘Doctor Pissington’. Then a friend offers him a job back in the artworld. He is to work on ‘The Floating World’, which is ‘a gated community beneath a giant dome on a desert island’ being built by a tech billionaire for the wealthiest as a refuge from climate crisis and political collapse. Our morally conflicted protagonist is hired to conduct research for an art exhibition marking the island’s inauguration. The novel negotiates the contradiction of inhabiting a contemporary artworld sustained by the good intentions of art workers who align themselves with beauty and virtue, while depending on the very forces their work purports to resist.

It opens with the narrator, in Ireland, on the verge of writing, before disappearing into his recollections, and eventually returns to the point at which the story is being written (more on which later). Grief provides its emotional landscape: the narrator’s reality is shot through with the frenetic despair that comes with the sudden loss of his wife. His grief gradually becomes entangled with the project of ‘The Floating World’ and the people making it, forcing a confrontation with the loss he has been carrying. It is in such experiences that resist ordinary expression that art becomes most meaningful: a painting, for example, that is ‘a truth that didn’t need explaining. No aristocrats, no symbolism, no lies. A painting clear as love’; and another, when the narrator’s friend likens the experience of pregnancy to a painting they once saw in a museum, in which ‘The colours are stronger and brighter, there’s a texture. It’s like breaking through a screen, the world feels bigger, like it can’t be contained.’

Eastham is at his most sensitive when criticism itself becomes inadequate. There is a pleasing irony in an art critic writing about an art critic for whom, and for the artists around him, the most profound encounters with art seem to occur precisely when interpretation fails. While Eastham is tender in his descriptions of art, his acute observations of the people surrounding it can be lacerating. He has a formidable talent for summoning up a character – or skewering one – in a sentence. One woman possesses ‘the erotic hauteur of an academic who in her youth danced beneath filtered spotlights at psychedelic happenings’. Another, ‘a woman in those oversized metal-rimmed spectacles designed to signal to civilians that the wearer is an intellectual’. Eastham is exacting not only when it comes to how people appear, but also about the identities they are trying, sometimes desperately, to project. Despite the grieving anguish of its narrator, it is his wry, deadpan humour that carries the novel. There is a dryly comic sparring match with a ‘philanthropist’ who believes happiness can be quantified, and a conversation between partygoers about where, literally, ‘the shit is going’. At times it is not unlike a drawing-room comedy, with its sharp wit, back-and-forth banter and clever insults.

The metafictional frame allows the novel to avoid the aftermath of its most dramatic events, dwelling instead on the act of remembering and reconstructing them. I’m not convinced this framing adds to the reader’s understanding of the narrator’s grief or the events being recounted. The narrator returns to remarkably similar emotional terrain at the end: melancholic and still lost, but perhaps slightly more hopeful for the future. For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, The Floating World remains surprisingly sincere about art itself. This is especially persuasive when Eastham uses art to give shape to experiences that elude explanation – love, pregnancy, grief – reminding us that beneath the bullshit posturing of the artworld is an unexpectedly earnest faith that art can make felt what we cannot quite articulate.

The Floating World by Ben Eastham. Fitzcarraldo Editions , £14.99 (softcover)

Copyright Nöel Manalili."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Olivier Marty, co-founder of the Paris-based architecture firm Studio KO, specializes in giving historic structures a considered second life. His latest project, the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent), does just that for the 1912 tram depot and diesel station in the heart of Uzbekistan’s capital, transforming it into the country’s first permanent institution dedicated to contemporary art."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Before Tashkent, Studio KO developed a distinctive approach to cultural buildings. The Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech (2017) is acclaimed for its restrained brick latticework and carefully controlled light, while the more recent Musée de la Mode et du Costume in Arles (2025) transformed an 18th-century townhouse into quietly elegant setting for one of France’s most extensive regional collections for textiles and costumes. Both projects reveal Studio KO’s preference for subtlety over spectacle, a design philosophy on full display in Uzbekistan."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Working with partner Karl Fournier, Marty chose to preserve, rather than overwrite, the building’s character. The main exhibition hall retains its original brick walls and vast proportions, a space they describe as “basilica-like.” A metal tunnel carries visitors into the galleries, while courtyards and subtle design elements nod to traditional Uzbek forms without turning decorative. The result is a contemplative environment flexible enough to house exhibitions, research, and public programs."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ahead of CCA Tashkent’s public opening, Marty spoke with ArtAsiaPacific about the thinking behind the transformation, and what it means for contemporary art in Central Asia."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/09/GLAS9911.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the eve of the CCA Tashkent’s unveiling, how has working within a 1912 tram depot and diesel station—a layered site shaped by imperial Russian, Soviet, and Central Asian histories—shifted your understanding of adaptive reuse as something more than heritage preservation? What does it mean to give a structure a “new poetic life,” in a city still negotiating between its modernist and vernacular indigenous identities?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It takes time—the time to give attention and sincerity to each layer. First, we identified the recent additions to the building: elements that imitated the historic details of the original features without having their qualities. This was a time of choosing, selecting, and filtering. Then, what was kept had to be renovated using techniques that had disappeared from the country decades ago—brick and joint treatment, zinc cladding on horizontal elements, and so on. Then we made the choice of legibility when creating the contemporary flow, through excavation and the construction of new elements. The materiality of all these additions was, deliberately, in total contrast with the existing architectural fabric. They are dark, with the feel of poured concrete, as opposed to the modular brickwork typical of imperial architecture."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/10/Muse--e-YSL-Marrakech_-STUDIO-KO__Cre--dits-Dan-Glasser--29-.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/10/Muse--e-YSL-Marrakech_STUDIO-KO_-Cre--dits-Dan-Glasser--13-.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Exterior views of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, Marrakech. Photos by Dan Glasser. Courtesy Studio KO."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Studio KO has long approached Morocco not as an exotic backdrop but as a laboratory of material intelligence, from the terracotta brickwork of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech to the earth and local craft traditions for private houses. How did these experiences of engaging climate, craft lineages, and cultural hybridity prepare you for the specific conditions of Tashkent?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We like to say that the Studio’s response is more an approach, an attitude, rather than a style. This is what we applied to this project: listen and observe a lot before making choices. The minerality of the country, the colors of the soil, the vernacular repetition of courtyards. In the end, there are similarities with our Moroccan projects, although the context is very different."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/09/GLAS0043.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/09/GLAS9994.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Installation views of TARIK KISWANSON ’s Nest , 2026 (left), and ALI CHERRI ’s A mouth, a wound , 2025 (right), at the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent. Depot Reborn: Interview with Olivier Marty of Studio KO

KARL FOURNIER (left) and

OLIVIER MARTY (right). Copyright Nöel Manalili.

Olivier Marty, co-founder of the Paris-based architecture firm Studio KO, specializes in giving historic structures a considered second life. His latest project, the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent), does just that for the 1912 tram depot and diesel station in the heart of Uzbekistan’s capital, transforming it into the country’s first permanent institution dedicated to contemporary art.

Before Tashkent, Studio KO developed a distinctive approach to cultural buildings. The Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech (2017) is acclaimed for its restrained brick latticework and carefully controlled light, while the more recent Musée de la Mode et du Costume in Arles (2025) transformed an 18th-century townhouse into quietly elegant setting for one of France’s most extensive regional collections for textiles and costumes. Both projects reveal Studio KO’s preference for subtlety over spectacle, a design philosophy on full display in Uzbekistan.

Working with partner Karl Fournier, Marty chose to preserve, rather than overwrite, the building’s character. The main exhibition hall retains its original brick walls and vast proportions, a space they describe as “basilica-like.” A metal tunnel carries visitors into the galleries, while courtyards and subtle design elements nod to traditional Uzbek forms without turning decorative. The result is a contemplative environment flexible enough to house exhibitions, research, and public programs.

Ahead of CCA Tashkent’s public opening, Marty spoke with ArtAsiaPacific about the thinking behind the transformation, and what it means for contemporary art in Central Asia.

On the eve of the CCA Tashkent’s unveiling, how has working within a 1912 tram depot and diesel station—a layered site shaped by imperial Russian, Soviet, and Central Asian histories—shifted your understanding of adaptive reuse as something more than heritage preservation? What does it mean to give a structure a “new poetic life,” in a city still negotiating between its modernist and vernacular indigenous identities?

It takes time—the time to give attention and sincerity to each layer. First, we identified the recent additions to the building: elements that imitated the historic details of the original features without having their qualities. This was a time of choosing, selecting, and filtering. Then, what was kept had to be renovated using techniques that had disappeared from the country decades ago—brick and joint treatment, zinc cladding on horizontal elements, and so on. Then we made the choice of legibility when creating the contemporary flow, through excavation and the construction of new elements. The materiality of all these additions was, deliberately, in total contrast with the existing architectural fabric. They are dark, with the feel of poured concrete, as opposed to the modular brickwork typical of imperial architecture.

Exterior views of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, Marrakech. Photos by Dan Glasser. Courtesy Studio KO.

Studio KO has long approached Morocco not as an exotic backdrop but as a laboratory of material intelligence, from the terracotta brickwork of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech to the earth and local craft traditions for private houses. How did these experiences of engaging climate, craft lineages, and cultural hybridity prepare you for the specific conditions of Tashkent?

We like to say that the Studio’s response is more an approach, an attitude, rather than a style. This is what we applied to this project: listen and observe a lot before making choices. The minerality of the country, the colors of the soil, the vernacular repetition of courtyards. In the end, there are similarities with our Moroccan projects, although the context is very different.

Installation views of TARIK KISWANSON ’s Nest , 2026 (left), and ALI CHERRI ’s A mouth, a wound , 2025 (right), at the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent. Photos by Dan Glasser. Courtesy Studio KO.

In both Morocco and Uzbekistan, you have approached brick not merely as a building unit, but as a carrier of memory and technique. For the 2023 Uzbekistan Pavilion at the Venice Architecture Biennale, “Unbuild Together: Archaism vs. Modernity,” you worked with students and artisans around the mud-brick qalas, or Zoroastrian desert fortresses, of Karakalpakstan. How did that research into archaic brick cultures inform your treatment of Uzbekistan’s industrial brickwork and the new insertions at CCA Tashkent?

The discovery of the qalas was more about showing the chronological porosity between archaism and modernity. Having been built so long ago, their volume and layout have so much abstraction; accessible from below, like our tunnel leading to the diesel station, made of masses like many of our interventions—there was so much to learn from there. There were many experiences too with terracotta brick in part two of the workshop; we made many exercises with them, of both layouts and finishes, natural or glazed.

Rendering (left) and installation view (right) of the Uzbekistan Pavilion at the 18th Biennale Architettura, Venice, 2023. Photo by Gerda Studio. Courtesy the Uzbekistan Art & Culture Development Foundation, Tashkent.

The Venice pavilion was conceived as a collaborative laboratory involving Uzbek students, scholars, and artisans. How did that pedagogical and co-creative model inform the design process for CCA Tashkent? How do you see the architect’s role shifting when a project becomes the platform for transmitting knowledge rather than simply delivering a finished object?

It is hard to explain, because these workshops happened in the very middle of the global process of CCA Tashkent, when most of the drawings were already done. But the diesel station had almost the same dimensions as the Arsenale pavilion in Venice. Chance or destiny? Before the renovation works, we installed in the diesel station a crazy one-to-one model of the Venice labyrinth. There is an echo, both geographic and civilizational. Watching those kids discover, in Tashkent, the replica of what would be installed in Venice was very moving.

SHOKRUKH RAKHIMOV ’s

The Colour of Silence, In Search of Truth , 2026, in the courtyard of the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA Tashkent). Courtesy Studio KO and CCA Tashkent.

The courtyard of CCA Tashkent is conceptualized as a contemporary version of a traditional mahalla , or residential community. How do you negotiate the tension between inventing a new communal spatial type and respecting the social and spatial logics of established Uzbek urban forms, particularly when designing a public cultural institution that aims to be both contemplative and open?

The enclosed space, big gate, perception of the surrounding construction and urban fabric—all of this is all the same, although the expression is different.

Your practice has always treated context as the starting point—from the desert light of Morocco, the maquis of Corsica, or the industrial fabric of Tashkent—rather than imposing a signature style from elsewhere. At a time when global cultural infrastructure often produces interchangeable “iconic” museums, how do you avoid homogenizing a place while working as architects across different continents?

I think it takes, on the one hand, a lot of modesty and respect for alterity, as well as a strong and confident vision on how to deal with it. Our years of practice have made this easier today, and clients come for this approach, which is very rewarding.

Interior views of the Musée de la Mode et du Costume, Arles. Photos by François Deladerrière. Courtesy Studio KO.

Having moved from designing private residences and the highly specific YSL museum to a major public cultural institution in a post-Soviet Central Asian capital, how has the scale and civic responsibility of CCA Tashkent changed your thinking about the relationship between architecture, cultural diplomacy, and the creation of new institutional “software” alongside physical form?

Scale-wise, even politically, there are many similarities, because the project serves a purpose combining altruism, power, and vision. But for the first time it is not dedicated to couture or textile like in Arles, but to artists. To watch them taking over the space you have designed for their installations is beautiful.

The main hall of the former diesel station has been described as a smaller version of the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. Rather than imposing a neutral white cube logic, you chose to honor the building’s industrial character while introducing a metal tunnel, courtyard, and other carefully calibrated interventions. What does it mean for a contemporary art institution in Central Asia to inhabit a space that still carries traces of its industrial and imperial past without erasing them?

It means that in this region there can be a path to modernity and development based on accepting the traces of the past, like existing buildings. It means a lot, both conceptually and practically. Uzbek authorities, at the highest level, now want to save a lot of buildings—it showed the way, maybe.

NADIA KAABI-LINKE ’s

Flying Carpets , 2011, at the Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent, 2026. Courtesy the Uzbekistan Art And Culture Development Foundation and Andrey Arakelykan.

Looking across the arc of your career leading to CCA Tashkent, how has your understanding of architecture’s afterlives—such as material sourcing, labor conditions, future reuse, environmental consequences—evolved? What specific afterlives do you hope this space will generate beyond its opening?

After a few super-intensive days leading up the opening, local users and teams have used every possible space and configuration! 5,650 visitors on the first day. Beyond photographs, honors, or prizes, this is the best afterlife we could dream of. Collective emotion.

Elaine W. Ng is editor and publisher of ArtAsiaPacific.
