article_text:
連続テレビ小説「ブラッサム」で、有力誌の編集者として主人公の珠（石橋静河さん）と関わっていく山中勇三。どんなキャラクターなのでしょうか。この役を演じる井浦新さんのコメントが届きました。

＜役柄＞山中勇三 黒崎の右腕。一流の作家を数多く抱える「首都公論」を、冷静な判断力で支える敏腕編集者。

「家族や親せきみんなに喜んでもらえる朝ドラ出演」

Q1 出演が決まったときの感想を教えてください。 井浦さん 『なつぞら』の時もそうでしたが、連続テレビ小説からのオファーというのは自分がうれしいだけではなく、親戚一同、家族みんなに喜んでもらえる本当に光栄なことです。 西尾一路役の染谷（将太）君とは『なつぞら』以来の共演になるので、また朝ドラで会うなんてちょっとおもしろいねと話をしました。他の映画やドラマに比べて1日で撮る分量が圧倒的に多く、撮影のリズムが速いので、緊張やプレッシャーも感じます。朝ドラのリズムの中にポンと入ってすぐにエンジンをかけられるか緊張しました。

「仕事や文学に情熱を傾ける」

Q２ 演じられる山中勇三はどんな役ですか？ 井浦さん まずは、遠藤憲一さん演じる黒崎編集長とのコンビネーションの中から山中の人物像を作っていきました。全くタイプが違う二人ですが、思ったことや感じたことをそのまま言葉と体に出す直感的な黒崎と、それ以外のものを持っている山中はとてもバランスがいいと思います。黒崎から山中への絶対的な信頼が見えますし、山中も編集長に対して結構ズケズケと物を言うので、ただの上下関係ではなく本当に信頼し合った戦友のような関係なのではないでしょうか。黒崎と対比すると山中は静と動の「静」ですが、いつも冷静沈着な精密機械のようなキャラクターというわけではありません。監督と相談しながら淡々としたセリフに少し肉づけをし、生っぽい言い回しに落とし込みながら役を育てました。細かなところで黒崎さんへの信頼や敬愛がにじみ出る、人間らしい揺らぎが表現できていたらいいですね。敬語と敬語じゃない時の使い分けが明確なところも、山中の特徴です。珠のような出自やキャリアの作家でも認めたらパッと敬語に切り替えますが、編集部員などにはまだ敬語ではありません。きっと山中なりのルールがあるのでしょう。意外とこういう部分が人間臭さにつながるので、大切にしています。敬語を使うのは作家への敬意はもちろん、自分の仕事や文学に対する山中なりの情熱の表れでもあると思います。

「飛びぬけた能力を持つ人への敬意が深い」

Q３ 山中は珠にどんな気持ちで接していると思われますか？ 井浦さん （第5週のシーンの）たまたま悠樂軒に来た黒崎編集長に原稿を手渡すという、ある種“飛び級”のような珠のやり方は山中好みではなかったと思います。文壇の世界は誰にでもチャンスが開かれているわけではありません。そこに“飛び級”のようなやり方で入ってくる珠のことが、山中は苦手だったのではないでしょうか。でも「苦手」ではあっても、「嫌い」ではないと思うんですよね。というのも、僕の中で「山中は面倒くさい人間が大好き」という設定があって、面倒な100のことはできないけれど1のことが飛び抜けてできる人や、山中自身が持っていない能力を持っている人への敬意が深いはずです。その最たる人が黒崎さんですが、きっと敵も多くてつきあうのも大変な黒崎のことを山中は大変だと思っていません。同じように、珠のことも実は大好物だろうなと解釈して演じています。山中は自分も変なことには気づけていないタイプ。周りから見れば山中も変なのに、黒崎や珠を「変な人ってやっぱりおもしろいな」と見ているんです。このわかりやすくはない変さや自覚のないオリジナリティが実は出ている、人としての豊かさも山中の魅力です。

「今の時代に刺激を与えられる朝ドラ」

Q４ 視聴者の方への見どころ・メッセージをお願いします。 井浦さん すごく挑戦的な朝ドラだなと思っています。人を愛することや恋をたくさんすることは、決して悪いことではないはず。でも、いまは「常識がない」「節操がない」という言葉で簡単に片づけられてしまう、そういう流れが色濃い時代になっているからこそ、刺激を与えられるのではないでしょうか。 これまでの朝ドラのヒロイン像とは少し違うかもしれませんが、情熱的に人を好きになることや愛すること、人と人とが関わり合うことの尊さを謳う（うたう）作品にきっとなると思います。珠の素直に人を愛して、恋をして、それを仕事にも生かして…という生き方が朝ドラというフィルターを通してどう表現されるのか僕も楽しみにしています。 (美術展ナビ編集班)

"画家猪熊弦一郎（1902—1993）是一位爱猫人士。从战中到战后，在最多的时候他曾同时养过一打猫，猫也因此作为新的母题出现在他原本以人物像为核心的画作中。他曾言：“以往各种各样画出来的猫，我总觉得都不太合心意。所以我便想用前人未曾尝试过的方法来描绘猫的形状和颜色。”这一时期正是通过对形与色之美丽平衡的探索，猪熊的绘画表现从具象过渡到抽象的转型期。因此，猪熊笔下的猫并不写实，而是融入了变形、分割为几何图形或仅用线条简单勾勒等独特表现。与此同时，画面中也自然流露出画家在共同生活中捕捉到的猫的自然身姿，仿佛从画笔中流淌出对猫的敬意与喜爱。本展在关注猪熊与猫之关系的同时，也将向大家介绍其独特的“猫表现”。", article_text:
丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館(MIMOCA、香川県) が2027年度の展覧会スケジュールを発表しました。

同館は2027年3月31日まで施設改修のため、休館中です。4月にリニューアルオープン後は、「第2回 MIMOCA EYE / ミモカアイ」「奥山由之展 大いなる矛盾／視線の行き交い」「中田真裕展 ( 仮 )」「 猪熊弦一郎と猫」の4展が予定されています。

同館は「2027年度は、次世代を担うアーティストに光を当てます」と宣言しています。若手の公募展や80年代、90年代生まれの二人のアーティストの展覧会を企画しているところからも、その姿勢は見て取れます。各展覧会の概要について、それぞれまとめました。（画像の無断転載をお断りします）

丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館(MIMOCA)

所在地：丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館（香川県丸亀市浜町80-1）

開館時間： 10:00～18:00（入館は17:30まで）※2027年3月31日まで休館中

休館日：月曜日、展示替え期間

観覧料： 企画展 • 一般：1,500円(団体：1,200円、市民：900円) • 大学生：1,000円(団体：800円、市民：600円) 常設展 • 一般：300円(団体：240円、市民：免除) • 大学生：200円(団体：160円、市民：免除)

アクセス： JR丸亀駅下車、南口より徒歩1分

詳細は、 丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館公式サイト まで。

第2回 MIMOCA EYE / ミモカアイ

2027年4月24日ー7月19日

「アートとはその時代の答えであって、アーティストはこの現代をどう表現するのかという責任がある。それがコンテンポラリーアート。未来に向かってアーティストがどういうふうに方向づけ、今にないものを発見していくかっていう、一番大事で一番難しいことの結果を見せる美術館であってほしい」ーー猪熊弦一郎

この言葉を指針とするMIMOCAでは、これからを担う若いアーティストが時代を捉えながら新しい表現を生み出し、独自の才能をはばたかせる起点となる場として、公募展「MIMOCA EYE / ミモカア イ」が2022年から実施されています。 第2回となる今回は、36歳以下のアーティストを対象に現代美術の作品を募集し、488人(組)から応募がありました。本展では、その中から選出された入選作品が展示されます。施設改修を経て生まれ変わったMIMOCAで、若いアーティストたちによる挑戦を鑑賞できます。 また、入選作品の中から大賞作品、選考委員個人賞を選出し、大賞受賞作家は、2028年度または2029年度にMIMOCAでの個展開催を予定しています。 ※入選作品の発表は2026年11月中旬、大賞および選考委員個人賞の発表は 2027年4月23日 を予定しています。

奥山由之展 大いなる矛盾／視線の行き交い

2027年8月7日ー12月5日

写真家・映画監督の奥山由之による、公立美術館初の個展です。写真と映画を起点に、多様なメディアを横断しながら独自の表現を切り拓いてきた奥山の15年以上にわたる活動を、350点を超える作品から捉え直します。 初期の代表作から現在までを再構成する「大いなる矛盾」と、近作の 〈flowers〉〈windows〉〈photographs〉の三部作を中心とする「視線の行き交い」の二つの軸で構成し、今後の展開を予感させる新作も交えて、その作品世界に迫ります。具象と抽象、現実と虚構、意識と無意識など、相反するものが共存する「矛盾」を手がかりに、世界を一面的に捉えることへの違和感や、他者との関係を見つめ直す奥山の実践を紹介します。 誰もがスマートフォンやAIによって容易に画像を生み出せる時代に、写真だからこそ可能な表現とは何か。本展は、写真というメディアの本質と、その新たな可能性を問いかけます。

中田真裕展(仮)

2027年12月18日ー2028年4月9日

伝統的な漆芸技法「 蒟醤 」を香川で習得し、その表現を一貫して追求してきた漆芸作家・中田真裕による、美術館での初めての個展です。 風や雲、水面など移ろいゆく自然や、記憶に刻まれた風景を題材に、独自の作品世界を築いてきました。蒟醤は、漆を塗り重ねた面に文様を彫り、色漆を埋めて研ぎ出す技法です。中田はこの工程を幾重にも重ね、豊かな色彩と奥行きを生み出すとともに、色層に反復される制作工程の痕跡と時間を蓄積させ、見る角度で表情を変える曲面によって、移ろいゆく風景を表現します。 本展では、新作を中心にこれまでの活動を辿り、瀬戸内の海や金沢の空など、作家の記憶から生まれた風景が、漆の表現を通して鑑賞者それぞれの記憶や感覚と響き合う世界を紹介します。香川の漆芸文化に根ざしながらも、伝統技法を現代の表現へと展開する中田の実践を通して、漆芸の新たな可能性に迫ります。

猪熊弦一郎と猫

2027年12月18日ー2028年4月9日

画家、猪熊弦一郎（1902‒1993）は愛猫家でした。戦中から戦後にかけて、多い時には一度に1ダースの猫と暮らしたこともあったそうで、そのうち人物像が中心だった彼の絵の中に、新たなモチーフとして猫が登場するようになりました。「今まで色々と沢山描かれている猫は、どうも自分には気に入らない。それで猫の形と色を今までの人のやらないやり方で描いてみたいと思つた」と述べています。 この時期は、形と色の美しいバランスの探求によって、猪熊の絵画表現が具象から抽象へと変わる過渡期にあたります。そのため、猪熊の猫の絵は写実的ではなく、デフォルメを加えたり、幾何学形に分割したり、線だけでシンプルに描くなど、独自の表現がみられます。同時に、ともに暮らすなかで画家の目がとらえた猫の自然な姿態もあらわれており、猫への敬意と愛情が絵筆から溢れ出ているようです。本展では、猪熊と猫の関係にも着目しつつ、その「猫表現」を紹介します。

2026年6月末から翌年3月末という9か月の長期休館を経て、MIMOCAが帰ってきます。この間、米ニューヨークのジャパン・ソサエティー（JS）・ギャラリーでの猪熊弦一郎展や、アーティスト・きむらとしろうじんじんとの長期プロジェクト「野点と丸亀妄想屋台群」など発信を続けていました。再開館後の意欲的な展覧会が期待されます。（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）

article_text:
Across some 200 booths at Art Basel Paris this year, there is a lot to take in. As the Swiss company’s French fair matures, galleries have begun to bring more and more top-tier, high-priced works, which in turn has made it less a place to discover something new than a place for six-, seven-, and even eight-figure works to be sold. And during the Avant-Première VVIP preview on Tuesday afternoon, exhibiting galleries reported quite a few sales, which they would add to by the close of business Wednesday.

While the fair can be a bit market-darling-heavy on the ground floor, be sure to visit the upstairs, where some of the best works on view can be found. And if nothing strikes your fancy, you can at least look up and take in the beauty of the Grand Palais’s green-painted, steel-and-glass ceiling.

Below, a look at the best booths at Art Basel Paris, which runs through October 25 at the Grand Palais.

Miyoko Ito at Ortuzar Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews In one corner of its booth, New York’s Ortuzar gallery has two striking abstract paintings from the mid-1970s by Miyoko Ito. Loosely associated with the Chicago Imagists, Ito has seen a posthumous resurgence in the past decade spurred in part by the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive’s 2017 survey of her work. (Ito attended the University of California, Berkeley, the home of that museum, in the 1940s and awarded her a diploma while she was imprisoned at the Topaz camp during World War II.) The works on view at Ortuzar’s booth show off her striking use of geometry; the dry application of thin layers of paint allowed her to achieve dazzling gradients.

Tatiana Trouvé at Xavier Hufkens Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews I haven’t stopped thinking about Tatiana Trouvé’s work since I saw her site-specific commission at the Upstate New York property of collectors Jill and Peter Kraus over the summer. It was a pleasant surprise, then, to learn that the bench that had drawn me into the center of Xavier Hukens’s booth (somewhere in the middle of the fair’s blue-chip axis) was by Trouvé, who is also currently the subject of a solo show at the Brussels gallery. This bench-like sculpture is part of her series on “The Guardian,” an unseen figure who is also the protagonist of her Kraus work. This bench is made from the fragments and skins of past work and the detritus of her studio (Styrofoam and blankets) that are then cast in aluminum and painted by hand. I didn’t dare sit on it, but somehow, I don’t think the Guardian would have minded.

Helen Frankenthaler at Yares Art Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews The spur of Art Basel’s fair is home to many of the secondary market galleries who have on view a range of historical works from the 20th century. But only one work from that section leaves an impression: Helen Frankenthaler’s Ivory Rose (1987). The purplish ground, achieved via the artist’s favored method of staining her canvas, contrasts with the thick paint that she applied on top: straight brush strokes of pure magenta, two circles of red-orange, an even vertical glob of slime green, and sprinkles of white. These two planes of color are a wonder. If only, I had the $1.6 million that the gallery is asking for.

Cem Örgen at The Pill Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews If you, like me, would rather see something new than a gallery’s inventory—essentially high-priced backstock, the action really gets going upstairs at Art Basel Paris. At Istanbul’s The Pill, Cem Örgen, who will feature in the New Museum Triennial next year, is showing two formally intriguing works. The artist studied industrial design at Bilgi University in Istanbul, and with these works, he subverts the functional aspects of his training to think about the fragility of the body. Horses (2024), for example, is a steel chair that can’t be sat upon; it takes its name from a small drawing affixed to the front of the logo of the artist pencil company Faber-Castell, showing two mounted warriors at battle. Open Surgery (2024), on the other hand, is made of Alucobond, a material that is typically used as the outer skin for buildings to help with insulation and acts as a fire retardant. The form of the work mimics the electrical wires that course through buildings and streets in our hyper-connected world. To these, he has added two silicon pads that are used in medical schools to train doctors on how to suture a wound. The tactility of Örgen’s sutures serves as a metaphor for the vulnerability that is just a slight movement in the wrong direction from bursting open in today’s media-addled society.

Carl-Edouard Keïta at Cecile Fakhoury Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews For his latest body of work, Carl-Edouard Keïta has turned his attention to the post-Independence period of his native Côte d’Ivoire. “It was a hopeful time,” he told ARTnews Wednesday morning. Using a Cubist-inflected sense of geometry to render the figures in his various scenes—from sporting events to dance clubs—Keïta draws on the past to offer a searing critique of the present. Les muses de l’Hôtel Ivoire (2026), for example, shows two Black women, elegantly dressed in ’70s garb, next to a traditional African sculpture. The artist saw that work at the Salon Art + Design fair in New York and was surprised to learn that it was from Côte d’Ivoire. Rendered at a 1:1 scale, it is the same height as the women. His research also led him to the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute, where he learned that it owns a dress designed by Karl Lagerfeld for Chloé in 1970 for a Texas socialite; the dress, for some reason, is titled Côte d’Ivoire. He has given that dress to the woman on the left, while the woman on the right wears a dress of his own design, an intervention into how an Ivorian woman from that era would dress herself.

Mary Stevenson and Ebun Sodipo at Chapter NY and Soft Opening Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews (2) This year’s edition of Art Basel Paris has a record 12 booths shared by two galleries. My favorite comes from Chapter NY and London’s Soft Opening. Both galleries have work on view by London-based artists whose work couldn’t be more different stylistically, though each artist’s practice deals with memory in its own way. Mary Stevenson’s Surrealist-inflected paintings explore psychological spaces: Red Chairs (2026), for example, shows five chairs floating in an almost star-like shape. The number five relates to her being one of five children and the way her siblings’ relationships encircle one another. To achieve this ethereal effect, she applies thin layers of paint to rabbit-skin-glue-primed linen. By contrast, Ebun Sodipo presents found images from her archive, which ranges from the art historical to the filmic to social media. She then mounts these onto Mylar and fixes them in time via two pourings of resin. By looking back at our collective memory, Sodipo proposes new futures for Black trans people.

Nina Davies at Seventeen Image Credit: Courtesy the artist and Seventeen, London I’m still not quite sure what to make of the two sculptures by Nina Davies in the presentation by New York’s Seventeen gallery. Both works, which hang from a single metal coat rack, are multi-part pieces that examine how dance “is disseminated, circulated, made, and consumed” in our current moment, per a release, specifically through the lens of AI. One work features a real-life dancer whose makeup and mannerisms make them seem AI-generated; during the video, Davies gives them movement instructions, written as though she were prompting an AI bot. The other presents a fictional podcast episode in which an investigative journalist details her findings on a bank break-in in which the thieves “physically reproduced AI-generated imagery to evade detection,” per a description from Vancouver’s Western Front, where the works premiered earlier this year. The devices these videos play on are stuffed into bags along with clothes, as well as sculptures of off-kilter Coke cans and disfigured hands, a nod to how AI-generated images often struggle to accurately render hands and brand logos.

Meriem Bennani at Lodovico Corsini Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews Don’t get too close to Meriem Bennani’s latest sculpture. More minimal than much of her previous output, A Knife (2026) presents a simple machine that moves a knife suspended from the ceiling up and down in a menacing fashion. Sculptured by Bennani, the knife seems as if it could drop at any second; the wooden armature below the knife, in fact, includes some marks where the knife seems to have landed. The sharpness of the knife contrasts with a rod that holds strands of blonde hair that resemble a feather duster. As ever, there’s an enigmatic humor to Bennani’s art that’s enticing—no matter how dangerous.

Rosario Aninat and Simon Shim-Sutcliffe at Eli Kerr Image Credit: Choreo The first Canadian gallery to participate in Art Basel Paris, Montreal’s Eli Kerr came to the French capital with a knockout booth. Because the booth is in the Emergence section, staged on the balconies that loom over the fair’s main floor, Kerr said he and the Berlin-based artist duo Rosario Aninat and Simon Shim-Sutcliffe chose to present something cinematic. Their booth has been overtaken by a sleek, black-painted bleacher inspired by a ziggurat. On this structure, they have placed around 15 discrete abstract sculptures that juxtapose different materials: cast tin and cast copper; padauk wood and epoxy clay; hand-blown glass and newsprint; Nero Assoluto granite, Belgian bluestone, and vulcanized rubber. Inspired by a recent research trip to China, where they encountered Neolithic objects, these pieces can be read as funerary objects that, in their amalgamation of materials, aim to meld heaven and earth. Each work also comes with a 35mm black-and-white photo (not on view) that acts as its certificate of authenticity.

Derek Jarman at Amanda Wilkinson Image Credit: Maximilíano Durón/ARTnews Tucked away in a corner of Art Basel Paris’s ground floor is the Premise section, for “highly singular curatorial proposals,” according to the fair’s website. The highlight here is London-based Amanda Wilkinson Gallery’s booth of Derek Jarman’s “Tar Paintings,” which he made between 1989 and 1991. Influenced by Carl Jung’s Psychology and Alchemy , Jarman brought an inherently alchemical sensibility to the way he transforms the sundry materials he covers in tar. When he started the series, Jarman was also at work on The Garden (1990), which features a scene in which someone is tarred and feathered. In that context, these aesthetically pleasing works take on a more serious tone, becoming a commentary on how HIV-positive people were treated during the AIDS crisis. Perhaps the most evocative of the works on view is Clothes (1989), featuring the blue overalls the artist would use for gardening, several found photographs, a set of clunky old metal keys, and other indiscernible objects. Onto this he has sprinkled feathers. Correction, October 22, 2026: An earlier version of this article misreported that Cem Örgen will have a solo show at the New Museum next year. He will, in fact, feature in the New Museum Triennial.

article_text:
Peter Medak , the Hungarian-born director and actor best known for films including “ The Changeling ,” “ The Krays ” and “The Ruling Class” died Tuesday in Los Angeles. He was 88.

Over a career spanning six decades, Medak directed 27 feature films, moving between psychological horror, black comedy and crime dramas. His 1980 supernatural thriller “The Changeling,” starring George C. Scott, won eight Genie Awards including best motion picture. He also directed the 1990 British gangster drama “The Krays,” for which he received the Evening Standard Award for best director.

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

Born in Budapest in 1937, Medak spent part of World War II in hiding with his family. Under Hungary’s Communist regime, his father was imprisoned and Medak was barred from attending school. He fled to England during the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and began working in the British film industry, eventually serving as assistant director before moving to Hollywood.

He made his feature directorial debut with 1968’s “Negatives,” starring Glenda Jackson. His 1972 satire “The Ruling Class,” starring Peter O’ Toole, competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes and earned an Oscar nomination for Toole. Other credits include “A Day in the Death of Joe Egg,” “Let Him Have It” and the Gary Oldman-led “Romeo Is Bleeding.”

Medak also worked extensively in television, directing episodes of “Homocide: Life on the Street,” “The Wire,” “Breaking Bad” and “House.” His 2018 documentary “The Ghost of Peter Sellars” revisited his troubled production of the 1970s comedy “Ghost in the Noonday Sun.”

He is survived by his four children, Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornela, and five grandchildren.

article_text:
“I definitely don’t think it is cringe,” says Laura Budds, a vintage furniture dealer based in Norfolk. “But I do think we have reached the peak, and we’re on the descent.” Budds is talking about mid-century modern furniture, which has recently come under fire from younger generations for being – like so many things, including trainer socks and high-waisted jeans – a deeply millennial aesthetic. As the Wall Street Journal declared : “Midcentury modern design has met the fate of pumpkin spice lattes, cocktails in mason jars, no-show socks, leggings and other aspects of millennial culture: it has become cringey.”

Budds, 44, is resigned to the fact that she is a “mid-century millennial”. She’s even made a career out of it: she sells furniture and vintage clothes at Williams & Parfitt , a modern antiques centre in Wymondham, Norfolk. But she says she has had to diversify in recent years to cater to changing tastes among younger customers, who are moving away from the “wall-to-wall mid-century” look beloved by the generation above them. She says of gen Z: “I don’t think they are so bound by the eras or designers – they just buy what they like. They aren’t afraid of older antiques and will have a bit of whimsy or taxidermy.”

The term “mid-century modern” was originally coined to refer to architecture and design that became popular from the 1940s to the 1970s, largely in the US, Brazil and Europe. Famed for its clean lines and simplicity, the style had visual forebears in the Bauhaus movement and classic Scandinavian design, along with the philosophy of beautiful yet functional furniture for the masses that spread to the US, UK and beyond in the postwar era. British-made items include Ercol and Robin Day chairs and G Plan teak sideboards, all of which are still coveted. (Anglepoise’s timeless industrial lighting, too, was associated with the aesthetic.)

The book Mid-Century Modern: Furniture of the 1950s, written by Cara Greenberg and published in 1984, is often seen as being responsible for popularising the phrase. Today, she says, the term has “become meaningless, applied to everything from museum-quality material to made-in-China repros on eBay”.

Greenberg lives in Brooklyn, New York. Her first mid-century purchase was an Eames plywood lounge chair bought at a street market in NYC in the 1970s, which she still owns. These days, she is more interested in a comfy sofa: “not a mid-century modern speciality”, she says, given the aesthetic’s tendency for furniture to be fairly upright and firm, often designed with polite conversation in mind rather than slouching and scrolling.

But, Greenberg says, she will still defend the best of it “as the most innovative and stylish furniture America ever came up with”: Charles and Ray Eames, the husband and wife duo who revolutionised design with multipurpose chairs; George Nelson’s industrial looks for the furniture company Herman Miller; Eero Saarinen’s Tulip chair for Knoll. Since then, she says, “there have been many cycles of revival, including the reissue and mass marketing of ‘best of’ classics by the original companies in the 1990s”.

Affordability has always been a cornerstone of mid-century design. “The philosophy of modernism and mid-century design, when it first started, was accessibility,” says Keith Stephenson, who lives in Camberwell, south-east London with his partner, Mark Hampshire. Together they run the design and homewares company Mini Moderns and co-authored the 2019 book Mid-Century Modern Living: The Mini Moderns Guide to Pattern and Style. “It was never supposed to be an elitist thing,” he says. “It was about bringing good design at a good price to as many people as possible. Reaching more people with good design is never a bad thing.”

It is also ideal for smaller spaces, which is one of the reasons Hampshire thinks it has “endured many a cycle of trends” to become “the endlessly go-to period of design”. The postwar period was “the first time that designers considered function and aesthetics together – so furniture was designed to solve a specific problem as well as to fulfil a function. The results of this level of considered design have, in many cases, proved hard to beat, thus becoming the template for subsequent designs.”

He gives an example: “If you look at a classic mid-century style sofa, it is on legs, so you can see the floor underneath it – and that makes a place feel much bigger, because you can read the room around the piece of furniture. There’s room to breathe. All of those things are classic interior design tricks to make a place look and feel more spacious.”

Mid-century modern’s design quality and price point made it irresistible to millennials who were starting to live independently in the 2010s. It fitted with the vintage aesthetic of the time and there were still bargains to be found. Even as late as 2019, says Budd, “you could find sideboards at auction for £50. Now you’re lucky to get one for less than £300-£400.” A lot of British mid-century modern has been shipped abroad in recent years, to Europe and as far as Japan, where consumers have cottoned on to British brands such as Ercol, G Plan and McIntosh. This has pushed prices up and “made it a bit too elitist. Only certain people can afford the really good quality stuff now,” says Budd.

The interior designer Natasha Landers has lived in her home in Walthamstow, east London, for 26 years. Her mid-century bookcase cost £30 when she bought it, and her £50 coffee table would now sell for £200. “It’s not as accessible as it was when I first started collecting,” she says. Still, she’s reluctant to write off the whole aesthetic just because it has been widely used. “Good design doesn’t have to become bad design because it is popular,” says Landers. “There is something slightly snobbish about deciding something is no longer cool simply because more people can enjoy it. What I do have a problem with is when everyone’s houses look the same.”

The proliferation of millennial style on the go-to interior design sources Pinterest and Instagram has inevitably meant that the high street and large webstores have capitalised on the trend. New furniture clearly inspired by classic mid-century modern pieces can now be found everywhere from Marks & Spencer and Dunelm to H&M and Temu.

“That craze for buying a full set of mid-century tables, sofas and lighting is definitely gone,” says Carina Harford , an interior designer from west London. “It had a paint-by-numbers experience to it that might have felt safe to its devotees but began to feel too commonplace.” The climate impact of “fast furniture” is also a consideration. “The imitation mid-century furniture that was coming out a lot in the last five or so years really irked me,” says Harford. “Stop buying new things if you don’t need them.”

It is this desire to avoid having identikit homes that is fuelling the mid-century modern cringe. “I really don’t want to have the same things as everyone else,” says Sheree Millington, a copywriter based in Margate, who is renovating her Victorian terrace. Lucy Hayes, a writer and director in east London, agrees. “I like a mix of styles and ages, and things that don’t feel rooted to a particular decade or era. I want my home to feel like it exists now rather than as a time capsule.”

Millington thinks a more quintessentially English style is coming back in, “whether that is cottagecore, or more like an English townhouse, with lots of mismatched things, more pattern, more print”. She is noticing chrome – a staple of 1990s homeware that has since fallen out of favour – becoming more popular again, too.

Harford’s home is kitted out with secondhand treasures spanning many different eras and styles: “It’s all just sort of mushed together, and I think it works.” Most of it was bought from auctions and cost about £100 or less. Highlights include a Victorian fold-out card table (bought for £110), lighting from a shuttered billiards hall (£40), a 1940s Anglo-Indian table (£30) and a set of 1980s stools (£90 for four). Although bidding can seem more complicated than buying new online for next day delivery, you quickly get the hang of it, she says, and the result is, “something much more special and unique”.

article_text:
Hot off a blockbuster 2026 between three hit movies, soon a fourth, plus an Emmy nomination, Zendaya has lined up her next acting project.

Details are under wraps, but the 30-year-old “Euphoria” and “Challengers” actor will next star in a new science-fiction film from writer/director Alex Garland at A24 , as the company announced on Thursday. The project will mark the British filmmaker’s fifth collaboration with A24, which distributed his debut directing effort “Ex Machina,” along with “Men,” “Civil War,” and “Warfare” (co-directed with former U.S. Navy SEAL Ray Mendoza). Garland wrapped production on A24’s most expensive in-house film production yet, the adaptation of the hit video game “ Elden Ring ,” earlier this year. The film is set for release in March 2028.

Production on Garland’s new science-fiction film will begin sometime in 2027, according to A24. Garland’s work in the genre dates back to collaborations with director Danny Boyle, including the outer-space thriller “Sunshine.” His directing efforts, from the artificial-intelligence thriller “Ex Machina” to the cosmic-horror movie “Annihilation” at Paramount, tend to hover around science-fiction themes. “Civil War,” which set A24 box-office records in 2024, imagined a fictional near-future collapse of the United States with sci-fi elements. At that point, it was A24’s costliest in-house movie.

Back in 2024 circa “Civil War,” Garland told IndieWire he’d be stepping back from directing for the “foreseeable future,” before a slew of behind-the-camera projects followed.

Zendaya, meanwhile, starred in three acclaimed films this year that grossed nearly $4.5 billion combined at the global box office: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” and A24’s “The Drama.” She also scored a Best Actress in a Drama Series Emmy nomination for “Euphoria,” which ended its three-season run earlier this year. Next up, she stars in “Dune: Part Three,” which looks to crash the Oscar race when it opens on IMAX screens starting December 18.

A24 hit the $200 million global box office milestone this year with “Backrooms,” and has opened a raft of other hits, including “The Drama” and, most recently, Robert Pattinson-starrer “Primetime,” throughout 2026 to company-record-setting success. The studio ended up outpacing Warner Bros. at the summer box office.

article_text:
Features

10 Years Later, Magenta Plains Is Still Embracing the Unexpected

An anniversary exhibition spotlights the artists who’ve made the gallery one of Lower Manhattan’s most adventurous success stories.

Olivia Smith had a thriving career running Exhibition A on the Upper East Side, a company that sells original contemporary art editions, when artists Chris Dorland and David Deutsch approached her in 2015 about opening a gallery on the Lower East Side.

Smith had worked with hundreds of artists producing limited edition prints, but she had never managed a commercial gallery or negotiated with museums before. Still, she felt a kinship with Dorland and Deutsch, who found a ground-floor storefront on Allen Street and needed help programming it. First they had to agree on a name, as long as it wasn’t their own on the door.

“We wanted something expansive and open-ended,” Smith told Hyperallergic . “We felt Magenta Plains represented a place, but we didn’t know what that place was that we were building yet.”

Hyperallergic )

A decade later, Magenta Plains has helped define what the Downtown contemporary art scene can offer the world. The gallery, which outgrew its original location and currently occupies a 4,500-square-foot space at 149 Canal Street, has featured groundbreaking technology-influenced installations, sculptures, and paintings, selections of which are on display in its 10 Year Anniversary show, up through October 31.

article_text:
Alexander Skarsgård knows how to make an entrance.

The Swedish actor has been turning heads with his wacky red carpet looks while promoting his new fantasy romance “ Wicker .”

At the London premiere earlier this month, he donned a metallic gold Saint Laurent suit. If that wasn’t bold enough, he slipped into a pair of clear plastic lace-up shoes.

Related Stories

‘Pixels and Pencils’ Panelists Talk the Dangers of AI, Demanding Animation Processes and the Importance of Human Creativity

Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato Recreate ‘Princess Protection Program’ Moments in New Rare Beauty Campaign

“They were surprisingly comfortable, and I was worried that they would steam up in five minutes, but that actually didn’t happen,” Skarsgård told me Saturday at the Academy Museum Gala. “But I’ve been getting a lot of comments from friends and family about my little piglets sticking out. They make fun of me. They make fun of my feet.”

Alexander Skarsgård says his clear shoes at the “Wicker” premiere were “surprisingly comfortable”: “I was worried they were going to steam up in five minutes.” #AcademyMuseumGala pic.twitter.com/EBivFxYpnU — Variety (@Variety) October 18, 2026

At the “Wicker” premiere in Los Angeles on Tuesday, Skarsgård wore a multicolored skirt and a whimsical black shirt adorned with his co-star Olivia Colman’s face from London fashion house Chopova Lowena. “We’ve been on a press tour for a couple of weeks, and now we’re in L.A., and it’s our final big premiere before the movie opens on Friday,” he said. “I wanted to wear something special for this lovely lady over here, Olivia, whom I adore.”

As for the purple and green skirt, Skarsgård said, “It’s very comfortable. It’s quite a hot night, and it’s light and breezy. I’m enjoying it.”

Earlier in the day, he shocked attendees at a SAG-AFTRA screening and Q&A when he arrived in a long gray wig . “I got a little jealous because everyone is complimenting Olivia on her beautiful hair and beautiful hair color,” Skarsgård said. “I got no love for my hair. As a narcissistic actor, I need a little bit of attention, so I threw on a beautiful gray wig to match Olivia today.”

“Wicker” co-star Elizabeth Debicki praised Skarsgård’s fashion choices. “He can do no wrong,” she said. “I love the man. What can I say? I’m biased.”

In “Wicker,” Colman plays an outcast in a medieval town who falls in love with a man made of wicker (Skarsgård). Debicki plays a housewife who burns with jealousy over the attention the townspeople give to Colman and Skarsgård’s characters.

Skarsgård’s wicker look was a practical costume created by the Wētā Workshop in New Zealand, with lead makeup effects artist Sarah Rubano, prosthetic designer Joe Dunckley and lead weaver Jasmin van Lith.

“Amazing,” Colman said of seeing Skarsgård in the costume for the first time. “We’d seen backward and forwards from Weta Workshop in New Zealand images for about 18 months, and so suddenly he puts it on, and we were all going, ‘Oh God, I hope it works.’ And he came out of the makeup trailer and went, ‘Oh God, it’s beautiful.’”

Olivia Colman says it was “amazing” to see Alexander Skarsgård in his wicker costume: “It’s beautiful.” pic.twitter.com/lFnjEnvZ5p — Variety (@Variety) October 21, 2026

“Wicker” is in limited release starting Oct. 23 before expanding on Oct. 30.

article_text:
古都・奈良の秋の風物詩、正倉院展。およそ1300年もの時を超えて守り伝えられた珠玉の宝物に出会えるこの展覧会は、今年で78回目を迎え、11月9日（月）まで奈良国立博物館で開催中です。ハカセとＮＡＲＩの２人も昨年の第77回に続いて駆けつけました。一体どんな宝物と出会えるのでしょうか。 正倉院宝物は、奈良時代の聖武天皇のご遺愛品を中心に、およそ9,000件もの品々が伝わります。もともと「正倉院」とは、公的な倉庫である「正倉」が立ち並ぶエリア全体のことを指し、全国各地に存在しました。東大寺にも複数の「正倉」があったのですが、長い年月を経て失われ、唯一残ったのが現在の正倉院なのです。

今年の正倉院展のメインヴィジュアルに採用されている「 漆胡瓶 」は、聖武天皇ゆかりの水差しです。ペルシア風の形でありながら中国・唐でつくられたようで、東西の文化交流を象徴する品なのです。漆塗りの表面には、シカや鳥、草花など多くの文様が描かれており、一つひとつ全ての文様を見てみたくなる美しさ。私は360度全ての向きから見てしまいました。

「 紅牙撥鏤碁子 」と「 紺牙撥鏤碁子 」が、それぞれ10枚ずつ展示されています。こちらも聖武天皇の愛用品。象牙を染めてから表面を彫って文様を表す 撥鏤 という技が使われています。こんなに小さな碁石に、花をくわえて飛ぶ鳥が緻密に表現されているのですから驚きです。聖武天皇が宮廷で碁を打つ姿をついつい想像してしまいます。

今回出陳されている「 虹龍 」は、近年の調査により、メスのニホンテンのミイラであることが判明しました。室町幕府第6代将軍の 足利義教 が宝庫に入って蘭奢待を切り取った際に、「 龍日干 」を見たとの記録が残っており、その際に雨が降ったことも記されています。この虹龍があることで、宝庫を開けるときはいつも雨が降るとされ、第3代将軍の足利義満が見たときにも雨が降ったそうです。ミイラとはいえ龍だけに、雨を降らす霊力を持つと考えられていたのでしょう。

外はあいにくの雨模様でしたが、雨の日に「虹龍」を見るという室町幕府の将軍たちと同じ体験ができたことに加え、「虹龍」の不思議な力で雨になったに違いないと、かなり興奮してしまいました。 古代の日本では、目に見えない霊的な存在が信じられていた時代でしたが、現代は科学技術の発達により、多くのことが合理的に説明できてしまう時代です。古都・奈良の地では、今も目に見えない何かが存在しているのかもしれない、そう思わせるに十分な展覧会体験で、非日常的な世界の広がりを感じた一日でした。（マンガ家・ＮＡＲＩ）

article_text:
恒星の向こう側

劇場公開日： 2026年10月30日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

国内外から注目を集める中川龍太郎監督が「走れ、絶望に追いつかれない速さで」「四月の永い夢」に続いて喪失と再生をテーマに撮りあげた3部作の最終章で、余命わずかな母のもとに帰郷した女性が、母と衝突しながらも彼女を理解していく姿を描いた人間ドラマ。 母の余命を知り故郷に戻った未知は、母・可那子に寄り添おうとするものの拒絶され衝突を繰り返す。未知は夫・登志蔵との子を身ごもっているが、亡き親友への思いに揺れる夫の姿に不安を募らせる。やがて母の遺したテープから“もうひとつの愛”を知った未知は、初めて母を理解し、母から託された愛を胸に前へと進んでいく。 「あの娘は知らない」の福地桃子が主人公・未知、「あん」「朝が来る」などの監督として知られる河瀨直美が母・可那子を演じ、寛一郎、朝倉あき、南沙良、三浦貴大、久保史緒里、中尾幸世が共演。劇場アニメ「ルックバック」のharuka nakamuraが音楽を手がけた。2025年・第38回東京国際映画祭コンペティション部門に出品され、福地桃子と河瀨直美がそろって最優秀女優賞を受賞した。

2025年製作／92分／G／日本 配給：NAKACHIKA 劇場公開日：2026年10月30日

article_text:
写真家・遠藤文香の作品展示が、東京・虎ノ門ヒルズ ステーションタワー4階の「虎ノ門 楽㐂（らっき）」で開催されている。写真集『Ayaka Endo: Kanoko』（7920円）の刊行を記念した企画「食べる、見る、読む。」として、2026年9月1日から10月31日まで、写真と文学、料理を横断する展示を展開する。

『Ayaka Endo: Kanoko』は、日本文学と現代写真を一冊の中で対峙させるシリーズの第6作。今回取り上げられたのは、歌人・小説家であり岡本太郎の母としても知られる岡本かの子の短編小説『鮨』だ。小説が写真の説明にならず、写真もまた小説の挿絵にならない。それぞれが独立した表現として向き合うことで、文学作品を新たな角度から読み直す試みとなっている。

遠藤は1994年生まれ。2021年に東京藝術大学大学院を修了し、現在はロンドンを拠点に活動する。動物や自然を主な被写体としながら、人間と自然のあいだに古くから存在する秩序や感覚に関心を寄せて制作を続けてきた。今回、店内では『Kanoko』の世界と呼応する写真作品を、食事を楽しみながら鑑賞することができる。

会場となる虎ノ門 楽㐂は、「NEXT JAPAN」をテーマに、江戸前寿司や旬の食材を用いた料理を提供する和食店。虎ノ門ヒルズ駅に直結する店舗で、通常のギャラリーとは異なり、食事と作品鑑賞が同じ空間で交差する。

さらに会期中は、岡本かの子の『鮨』と遠藤の写真世界から着想したスペシャルディナーコースも用意。前菜、刺身、焼物、揚物、握りなどで構成し、『Ayaka Endo: Kanoko』1冊が付属する。作品を「見る」、小説を「読む」、そして料理を「食べる」という3つの行為を重ねることで、一冊の写真集を視覚だけではなく味覚や身体感覚へと拡張する。価格は15000円。

ギャラリーや美術館を離れ、日常的に人々が食事をする場所へ写真を持ち込む今回の試み。岡本かの子が「鮨」という食を通して描いた文学世界に、遠藤の写真と現代の料理が重なることで、写真を見るという行為そのものを別の角度から捉え直す機会となりそうだ。

タイトル

遠藤文香「食べる、見る、読む。」

場所

虎ノ門 楽㐂（東京都港区虎ノ門2-6-3 虎ノ門ヒルズ ステーションタワー4F）

会期

2026年9月1日（火）〜10月31日（土）

時間

11:00～14:00（L.O. 13:30） 17:00～23:00（L.O. 料理22:00 ドリンク22:30、日曜日・祝日22:00までL.O. 料理21:00 ドリンク21:30）

休み

無休
